oneLiner.en: At a Zos Chanukah gathering the Mashgiach gives his chaburah practical advice on learning, davening, Chofetz Chaim and Shabbos, and explains the Chanukah lights as the chinuch of the light of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by thanking Hashem and, with Yosef's words to his brothers and the Ba'al Shem Tov, says that wherever a person is sent he has something to repair. Then he offers advice. He asks the chaburah to learn at night where they daven. He describes tefillah rising through the worlds to Shemoneh Esrei and the descent of the bounty afterwards, comparing one who leaves early to a shopper who pays and leaves his bag on the counter. Following the Imrei Emes's letter, he urges learning two halachos of Chofetz Chaim daily with a chavrusa, and suggests Shabbos gatherings and using shalosh seudos. On Chanukah he brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the lights are the chinuch of the light of Moshiach, and reads the nations' outcry against Jewish ownership of Eretz Yisroel through Rashi's first comment as a reason for joy. He closes with blessings for unity.

en: Where a person is sent is a sign from Hashem that he has something to repair there and a shlichus to fulfill.
The Mashgiach asks that the chaburah learn in the same beis medrash where they daven, with a fixed place for both tefillah and Torah.
The bounty gathered in Shemoneh Esrei descends in the parts of davening after it, so one should daven the whole davening and not leave early.
The Mashgiach proposes that each person learn two halachos of Chofetz Chaim daily with his chavrusa, finishing the sefer in a year.
The Chanukah lights lit generation after generation are the chinuch of the light of Moshiach, which will then be revealed in full.

title.en: Sent to repair; learning where one davens

summary.en: The Mashgiach thanks Hashem and, citing Yosef's words to his brothers and the Ba'al Shem Tov, says that where a person is sent is a sign he has something to repair there. Saying he will give advice rather than derashos, he asks the chaburah to learn at night in the beis medrash where they daven, as the Rebbes taught.

title.en: Tefillah rising through the worlds

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how davening rises from world to world, from pesukei dezimra to Shemoneh Esrei, where one stands before the King and asks for parnassah, refuos and everything. He tells of a man who davened there that a household helper not leave, and answers that one davens according to the plain meaning: to whom else should he ask?

title.en: The descent of the bounty after Shemoneh Esrei

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the bounty gathered in tefillah descends at Tachanun, Uva Letziyon and Aleinu, and compares one who leaves before then to a shopper who pays and leaves his bag on the counter. He rejects the claim that this is unnecessary, says it is not his own stringency but comes from great tzaddikim, and asks that people daven the whole davening.

title.en: The Imrei Emes and the sefer Chofetz Chaim

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the chaburah once all learned the same sefer so they could discuss it, and now urges learning Chofetz Chaim. He tells how the Imrei Emes wrote a letter to his chassidim to learn it, saying he felt its benefit himself, and thereby broke the divide between chassidim and Litvaks; the Mashgiach adds that learning it made him a different person.

title.en: Two halachos a day with a chavrusa

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that holding back a forbidden word at every moment is constant yiras shamayim and conquest of the yetzer, a great nachas ruach to Hashem. He proposes two halachos a day with one's chavrusa, at the start or end of learning, and suggests Rabbi Shimon Finkelman's English book for learning at home with the family.

title.en: Shabbos gatherings and shalosh seudos

summary.en: After asking for a refuah shleimah, the Mashgiach speaks of feeling a sweetness in Shabbos. He remembers Friday nights as a young man, when ten or fifteen Jews sat together telling stories of tzaddikim and singing zemiros, the high point of his week, and urges coming together and using the hour of shalosh seudos, which makes a person better.

title.en: Chanukah lights and the light of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Chanukah lights are the light of Moshiach, and that the lights Jews kindle generation after generation gather until it is revealed in full; the Bnei Yissaschar calls them its chinuch. He then reads the nations' outcry that the Jews are robbers in Eretz Yisroel through Rashi's first comment on Bereishis, and says it is a reason to rejoice.

title.en: Blessings for unity and the third Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach blesses the gathering that, with the power of Chanukah, the honor of Heaven be revealed and the third Beis HaMikdash be built, with yeshuos, refuos and simcha. He stresses that love and friendship among Jews bring blessing, cites Rabbi Akiva's great principle and the tefillah of Rebbe Elimelech to see the good in one's fellow, and ends with l'chaim.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Zos Chanukah, the eighth day, seals the judgment of Yom Kippur and corresponds to Moshiach, and that it is a time to hope for the redemption and to daven.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that on Zos Chanukah, the last day of Chanukah, a simple Jew can achieve through prayer what a tzaddik achieves on Rosh Hashanah. It is accepted that this is the time of gmar chasima tova, when the sealing of Yom Kippur ends, and the eighth light corresponds to Moshiach. There is an obligation to await Moshiach at every moment; at the judgment one is asked whether he hoped for the redemption, and 'for Your salvation we hope all day', said three times daily, gives the answer. The Rambam speaks of awaiting, not only believing. He then reads the Yalkut about the year Moshiach is revealed, when the kings of the nations provoke one another and Israel is told not to fear. He concludes that Jews must daven, since prayer can annul decrees, and asks everyone to say l'chaim with gmar chasima tova.

en: What a tzaddik can achieve through prayer on Rosh Hashanah, a simple Jew can achieve on Zos Chanukah.
It is accepted among Jews that Zos Chanukah is the time of gmar chasima tova, when the sealing of Yom Kippur comes to its end.
Zos Chanukah, the eighth light, corresponds to Moshiach, so it is a time especially suited to hoping for him.
There is an obligation to await Moshiach at every moment, and one is asked at the judgment whether he hoped for the redemption.
The Yalkut describes the year Moshiach is revealed as a time when the kings of the nations provoke one another, and Israel is told not to fear.
Jews must daven, since prayer can annul decrees, even harsh ones.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches that doubts in emunah are defeated by ignoring them, and then learns the Rambam's halachos of Moshiach, explaining why one who does not wait for him is a kofer and why a Moshiach without miracles is the greatest wonder of all.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins by comparing doubts in emunah to mazikim, harmful spirits that are real but have no true power. Following Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk, he says one must not argue with them but ignore them, as one nullifies chametz and as Avraham Avinu threw dust at the kings. Pushing such thoughts away fulfills the mitzvah of emunah, and like the geulah, a person's private exile has an end that Hashem can hasten. He then turns to the Rambam's Hilchos Melachim, chapters 11 and 12. He asks why one who believes in Moshiach but does not wait for him is a kofer, and answers that real belief in the promised good would bring longing, as with the Yismach Moshe. He shows Moshiach in the Torah, explains Rabbi Akiva and Ben Koziva, the difference between presumed and certain Moshiach, and argues that the Rambam's Moshiach without miracles is the greater wonder.

en: Doubts in emunah are like mazikim: one defeats them by ignoring them and declaring them nothing, not by arguing with them.
Pushing away such thoughts is not a sin but a chance to fulfill the mitzvah of emunah, which is a tikkun for all sins.
According to the Rambam, one who does not wait for Moshiach is a kofer, because true belief in the promised good would make a person long for it.
In every generation there is a Jew who could be Moshiach if the people merit it; Ben Koziva was such a person, and his death showed he was not Moshiach.
The Rambam distinguishes between one who is presumed to be Moshiach and one who is certainly Moshiach, like the halachic difference between a chazakah and certain knowledge.
The Mashgiach argues that a Moshiach who gathers all of Jewry and builds the Beis HaMikdash, with everyone accepting his word, is a greater wonder than the miracles the Raavad expects.

title.en: Ignoring the mazikim of doubt

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares thoughts of doubt to mazikim, real but powerless, and brings the advice of Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk to ignore them rather than argue. He links this to the strictness of chametz, which symbolizes the yetzer hara and is removed by declaring it nothing.

title.en: Dust on the kings and a private geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham Avinu defeated the kings by throwing dust, treating them as nothing, and says the doubts will pass and emunah will shine brighter. Ignoring them fulfills 'lo sasuru' and the mitzvah of emunah, and Hashem can shorten a person's trial as with the geulah; he closes with a brachah for Yom Tov.

title.en: The Rambam's halachos of Moshiach

summary.en: Opening a new shiur, the Mashgiach notes that the Rambam ends his Yad HaChazakah with the halachos of Moshiach in Hilchos Melachim chapters 11 and 12, so that one knows how to fulfill the belief in Moshiach and how to recognize him. He reads that one who does not believe in him or does not wait for him is a kofer.

title.en: Why not waiting makes one a kofer

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why a comfortable man who believes in Moshiach but is not interested is called a kofer, and answers from the Rambam's description of the bounty of the days of Moshiach: one who truly believed would long for him. He tells of the Yismach Moshe and the Chafetz Chaim waiting for Moshiach and points to the words of davening.

title.en: Moshiach in the Torah

summary.en: Following the Rambam, the Mashgiach shows the promise of Moshiach in Parshas Nitzavim and in Bilaam's prophecy in Balak, noting that the Torah does not fear to predict. He remarks that Balak is read as the Three Weeks begin, mentions the three added cities of refuge, and says one should not think Moshiach must perform miracles.

title.en: Rabbi Akiva and Ben Koziva

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Rabbi Akiva declared Ben Koziva, a powerful and righteous king who fought Rome, to be Moshiach, and how his death showed he was not. He explains that Rabbi Akiva did not truly err: in every generation there is a potential Moshiach, as the Gemara says of Chizkiyahu, and the people's sins spoiled it.

title.en: Presumed Moshiach and certain Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the next lines of the Rambam were removed by censors and restored from uncensored editions and manuscripts. Explaining chazakah with examples of meat and shechitah, he shows that a king from Beis David who learns Torah and fights Hashem's wars is presumed Moshiach, while one who builds the Beis HaMikdash and gathers Jewry is certainly Moshiach.

title.en: The greater wonder of the Rambam's Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Raavad's dispute that Moshiach will show miracles and clarifies that the Rambam only says miracles are not required. He then argues that a Moshiach whom all Jews follow to Yerushalayim, and who settles the exact place of the mizbeach so that all accept it, is the greatest wonder, and closes with wishes for the summer.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shabbos is Hashem's personal gift to Klal Yisroel, and that a Jew must prepare for it all week, through tefillah, kedushas habris, guarded speech, learning its halachos and honoring its food, in order to feel it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that Hashem called Shabbos a good gift from His treasury and told Moshe to make it known, and explains with the parable of a chasan's flawless diamond that Shabbos is a personal sign between Hashem and Klal Yisroel. He then shows that the whole week revolves around Shabbos: every mitzvah and tefillah prepares for it, a Jew should long for it, and its fire must be kindled during the week. He teaches that Shabbos is reached through kedushas habris, that erev Shabbos is the day of Yosef and yesod, and that people who do not feel Shabbos did not prepare for it. He describes how the whole Shabbos davening, the seudos and the fish must feel like Shabbos, that Shabbos is a name of Hashem and is emunah, and that it must be guarded in speech. He closes with learning hilchos Shabbos and the holiness of Shabbos food.

en: Shabbos differs from every other mitzvah: it is a personal gift and a sign of the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisroel, and a Jew must know its worth.
All the mitzvos and tefillos of the week revolve around Shabbos and are a preparation for it.
Kedushas habris, guarding the mind and the eyes, is what brings a Jew to feel the holiness of Shabbos.
Those who do not feel Shabbos have not prepared for it during the week with kedushah and Torah.
Shabbos must be guarded in speech, because Hashem's work in creation was through speech.
The food of Shabbos carries great holiness, the holiness of the mann, and must be eaten in honor of Shabbos.

title.en: Shabbos, the gift from Hashem's treasury

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that Hashem told Moshe He has a good gift in His treasury called Shabbos and that he should make it known, and asks why only Shabbos needed this. He answers with the parable of a chasan who sends his kallah a flawless diamond and must tell her it is not glass: Shabbos is a personal sign between Hashem and Klal Yisroel.

title.en: The whole week revolves around Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every mitzvah and tefillah of the week prepares for Shabbos and that a Jew should long for it like a chasan and kallah await the chuppah. He tells of chassidim leaving a melave malka at dawn who were greeted with the news that in six days it will be Shabbos again, recalls the European question whether a Jew 'has for Shabbos', and reads 'lo s'vaaru esh' as a call to kindle the fire of Shabbos during the week.

title.en: Praying for Shabbos; kedushas habris

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a Jew should pray constantly to merit a bright Shabbos and its oneg, and mentions R' Aharon of Karlin's song of longing for Shabbos. He teaches that the holiness of Shabbos is reached through kedushas habris, guarding the mind and the eyes in a world sunk in impurity, and that a warm Shabbos is a sign that one withstood such a test.

title.en: Erev Shabbos is the day of Yosef

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the six weekdays correspond to six sefiros and that erev Shabbos is Yosef, middas hayesod, through which one prepares for Shabbos. He brings Chazal that Yosef kept Shabbos in Mitzrayim, describes the 'bechinah of Yosef' as a Jew careful about what he eats, and says that one sunk in kelipos cannot feel Shabbos, as people complain to him.

title.en: Preparation and the Shabbos tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one does not feel Shabbos because one did not prepare all week with kedushah and Torah. He brings the Panim Yafos that the whole Shabbos Shemoneh Esrei, not only its middle berachah, and the whole davening must feel like Shabbos, a tzaddik's teaching that at Nishmas one davens with the soul alone, and that teshuvah, from which the name Shabbos comes, brings a Jew close to Shabbos.

title.en: The Shabbos seudos; Shabbos as Hashem's name

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one eats all week to have strength to learn and daven and so to taste the Shabbos seudos, and tells of an old chassid who asked Hashem to give him Shabbos in the challah and in the fish. He brings the Zohar that Shabbos is a name of Hashem, so ehrliche Yidden avoid saying the word in an unclean place, explains that Shabbos is emunah, and urges davening to guard Shabbos.

title.en: Guarding Shabbos in speech; the Shabbos home

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains from the passuk that Hashem rested on the seventh day that His work in creation was speech, so a Jew must guard Shabbos by measuring his words and not talking business at the seudos, but Torah, stories of tzaddikim and a word on the sedra. He describes the Shabbos home, kavod habayis, and the Shabbos lights as honor and shalom bayis.

title.en: Hilchos Shabbos and the holiness of Shabbos food

summary.en: The Mashgiach urges learning hilchos Shabbos, at least from kitzurim, and seforim on the greatness of Shabbos such as the Sidduro shel Shabbos. He describes how ehrliche Yidden have in mind the holiness of Shabbos in every spoonful, tells of R' Dovid Biderman eating a spoiled cholent rather than shame Shabbos food, says the food of Shabbos holds the holiness of the mann, and closes with a gut Shabbos.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the three ascending stages of Shabbos, culminating in Shabbos mincha and shalosh seudos, a time of yichud beyond place and time, and says one must want and pray to truly feel Shabbos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the three parts of Shabbos: Friday night, Shabbos morning and Shabbos mincha, which parallel the three parts of the Beis Hamikdash and the stages of kiddushin, nisuin and yichud. Each part has its tefillah and its seudah, and the Avos come as guests to our seudos, so the table should be run to please them. Mincha is the highest point: its Amidah has no pesukim, its seudah is simple, and it is a 'nachalah without boundaries'. Through a question of the Avnei Nezer about the manna kept in the Kodesh Hakodashim, he shows that what is beyond place is beyond time, and so is shalosh seudos. The time itself is a mikveh, Moshe Rabbeinu passed away then, and the Ba'al Shem Tov had it eaten together. He ends with the mashal of the weary traveler, the story of R' Shlomo of Karlin's sock, and the call to want to feel Shabbos.

en: Shabbos has three stages, Friday night, Shabbos morning and Shabbos mincha, like the courtyard, the Heichal and the Kodesh Hakodashim, and like kiddushin, nisuin and yichud.
The Avos come as guests to the three seudos, so the seudah should be conducted to please the guests, with divrei Torah, joy and warmth.
Shabbos mincha and shalosh seudos are beyond place and time, the yichud of Hashem and Klal Yisrael, like the Kodesh Hakodashim.
The higher the kedushah of Shabbos, the less it is felt, so Friday night is felt most and mincha least.
One must want to feel Shabbos and ask Hashem for it; keeping Shabbos without trying to feel it leaves a person like a wooden bench in Gan Eden.

title.en: The three stages of Shabbos

summary.en: Citing the Nesivos Shalom, the Mashgiach divides Shabbos into Friday night, Shabbos morning and Shabbos mincha, compares them to the three parts of the Beis Hamikdash and to kiddushin, nisuin and yichud, and explains that each tefillah prepares for its seudah.

title.en: The Avos as guests at the seudos

summary.en: From the Zohar the Mashgiach links the three seudos to Yitzchak, Avraham and Yaakov, who come as guests, and says the table should be run for the guests: divrei Torah, simcha, and a warm, relaxed atmosphere the children can enjoy.

title.en: Mincha without pesukim, a portion without bounds

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the three Shabbos Amidos differ: Friday night and morning contain pesukim, but mincha is short and has none, because it is above pesukim; shalosh seudos is likewise a simple meal, and the Zohar ties it to the 'portion of Yaakov', a portion without boundaries.

title.en: The Avnei Nezer on the manna: beyond place and time

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Avnei Nezer's question how the jar of manna could be kept before Hashem when manna may not be left over till morning, and his answer that place and time are one: the Kodesh Hakodashim, where the Aron took no space, was beyond time too. Shalosh seudos is likewise beyond time until bentching.

title.en: Yichud, the Kodesh Hakodashim and the mikveh of time

summary.en: Shalosh seudos is the yichud of Hashem and Klal Yisrael, like the Keruvim in the Kodesh Hakodashim where no one else may be. The Mashgiach asks why no tevilah is mentioned before Shabbos mincha and answers that the time itself is the mikveh, as on Yom Kippur; Jews together are a mikveh, which is why the Ba'al Shem Tov had shalosh seudos eaten together. Mincha is the chosen time of Shabbos and an eis ratzon.

title.en: Brich Shmei, Moshe's passing, and feeling the kedushah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the heavens open when the Aron is opened, above all at Shabbos mincha, and that Moshe Rabbeinu passed away at Shabbos mincha, a place beyond human measure, so no one knows his burial place. He brings the Toldos Yaakov Yosef that shalosh seudos alone is like weekday, and explains why the higher kedushah of the morning and of mincha is felt less than Friday night.

title.en: The taste of Shabbos and the weary traveler

summary.en: Like the manna, Shabbos tastes according to one's desire for it. The Mashgiach brings the Slonimer tzaddikim's mashal of a soaked, freezing traveler who reaches a warm inn to regain strength, as Shabbos restores a person for the week's avodah, and explains that time and place set the worth of a mitzvah, so Torah and mitzvos on Shabbos are of another order.

title.en: R' Shlomo of Karlin's sock, and wanting to feel Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how R' Shlomo of Karlin felt that his foot in a weekday sock did not feel Shabbos, and his warning that one who keeps Shabbos without trying to feel it will be like a wooden bench in Gan Eden. He speaks of gathering on Friday night to sing, of Klal Yisrael as the partner of Shabbos, of the difference between oneg and simcha on Shabbos, and closes with a tefillah before Shabbos Chazon.

oneLiner.en: Starting from the Gemara's rule that a poor man chooses the Shabbos light over the Chanukah light because of shalom bayis, the Mashgiach explains why the Rambam places the husband's duty to yield to his wife in the laws of Chanukah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara: one who has money for only one light takes the Shabbos light over the Chanukah light because of shalom bayis. Following Rashi, shalom bayis means not eating in the dark, which is oneg Shabbos, and since oneg Shabbos rests on the Torah's mikra kodesh, it outweighs the rabbinic pirsumei nisa. The Rambam, however, holds oneg Shabbos is rabbinic, so he follows the Meiri's second explanation: the wife lights the Shabbos candles, and the husband must give her the mitzvah so they do not quarrel. He draws practical differences, then shows from the Gemara in Yevamos and from Avraham's tent that the husband must be the one who yields. Peace at home mirrors and arouses the bond of Hashem and Knesses Yisrael. Since the Chanukah light shows Hashem's love, coming into each Jewish home, the Rambam placed this teaching in the laws of Chanukah.

en: According to Rashi, the shalom bayis of the Shabbos light means not sitting and eating in the dark, which is oneg Shabbos, a Torah-level matter that the rabbinic pirsumei nisa of Chanukah cannot push aside.
The Rambam, who holds that oneg Shabbos is not from the Torah, explains with the Meiri's second approach: the wife lights the Shabbos candles, and taking the mitzvah from her would cause strife.
Shalom bayis has such power that the Torah allowed Hashem's Name to be erased for it, and the whole Torah was given to make peace in the world; therefore it overrides the Chanukah light.
When there is a conflict at home, the husband must be the one who yields, honoring his wife more than himself, as the Gemara in Yevamos teaches and as Avraham pitched his wife's tent first.
The relationship of husband and wife is a mashal for the bond between Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, and peace at home arouses peace and blessing above.

The Rambam put the husband's yielding in the laws of Chanukah because the Chanukah light, like the Menorah of the Mikdash, testifies to Hashem's love for Israel, and on Chanukah Hashem comes into every Jewish home.

title.en: Shabbos light or Chanukah light

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that one who can afford only one light takes the Shabbos light because of shalom bayis, and explains with Rashi that shalom bayis means the household should not sit in the dark. He distinguishes this from the separate rule, a few pages later, of a light in every room so no one trips.

title.en: Why Rava calls it obvious

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Gemara finds it obvious that the Shabbos light wins, when pirsumei nisa overrides other mitzvos. He answers from the Shulchan Aruch HaRav and the Ramban that oneg Shabbos is from the Torah, via mikra kodesh, and a Torah mitzvah comes before pirsumei nisa, while kiddush over wine is only rabbinic.

title.en: The Rambam and the Meiri's second explanation

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the last halacha of the Rambam's laws of Chanukah, which grounds the preference in the greatness of peace. He brings the Meiri's second explanation: the wife lights the Shabbos candles, and if the husband spends the money on his Chanukah light there will be no peace, and says the Rambam learns the Gemara this way.

title.en: Why the Rambam must learn it this way

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Rambam departs from Rashi and the other Rishonim, and answers that the Rambam holds oneg Shabbos is not from the Torah. He then asks why rabbinic shalom bayis should override pirsumei nisa, and answers from the Rambam's words that peace has a tremendous power, for which even Hashem's Name may be erased.

title.en: Practical differences; why the husband yields

summary.en: The Mashgiach draws differences between Rashi and the Rambam: by the Rambam the wife may waive her claim, and a man without a wife would light the Chanukah light. He then asks why the husband, not the wife, must give in, and answers from the Gemara in Yevamos that a man honors his wife more than himself, with Rashi's proof from Avraham's tent.

title.en: Husband and wife as a mashal for Hashem and Israel

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the bond of husband and wife is a mashal for Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, so peace at home arouses peace above, and every kindness a Jew does arouses Hashem's kindness, as in the Tomer Devorah. From Shir HaShirim and Avraham's tent he shows that Hashem too, so to speak, honors Knesses Yisrael more than Himself.

title.en: The tefillah for shalom bayis and bearing with others

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells that a Lithuanian gadol answered that the tefillah for shalom bayis is the request in davening that one's soul be like dust, to yield and bear with others. He mentions the patience of the gabbai of Reb Shlomo of Zvhil, then explains from the Tomer Devorah that Hashem bears with the sinner, and one who bears with others at home arouses this above.

title.en: Why in the laws of Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Rambam lists the duties of husband and wife in the laws of Ishus but leaves out the husband's yielding, placing it instead in the laws of Chanukah. He explains that the Chanukah light is modeled on the Menorah of the Mikdash, a testimony that the Shechinah rests in Israel, and reads the Rambam that the Chanukah light is a very beloved mitzvah.

title.en: Hashem comes into the home; chanukas habayis

summary.en: Following the Sfas Emes, the Mashgiach explains that every Chanukah menorah makes the home a Mikdash: instead of the Jew coming to the Mikdash, Hashem comes to him, showing He honors Knesses Yisrael more than Himself, which is why the Rambam placed shalom bayis there. He closes at the chanukas habayis of his grandson Shmuel Yehuda with a brachah that the home be a dwelling for the Shechinah.

catalogTitle: Our Generation's Unique Need to Stress the Truthfulness of the Torah

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why the truth of the Torah rests on the revelation at Har Sinai before millions, unlike religions built on the word of one man, and why the Torah can never be changed.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that a person must accept, and even thank Hashem for, whatever He sends, and that today's bochurim, exposed to the world and its media, need hashkafah. His subject is the truth of the Torah. Both Christianity and Islam must accept Toras Moshe and only claim it was changed, because of what happened at Har Sinai. He describes how each of these religions began with one man, and how their founders removed the difficult mitzvos, since only Hashem could make a promise like that of shemitah. At Sinai, by contrast, Hashem spoke to millions, and the Torah written for that generation could not have contained a lie; it has come down letter for letter. History seen by multitudes cannot be faked, as with George Washington. He ends that the Torah is forever and Hashem, who knows the future, does not change His mind.

en: The Mashgiach says that both Christianity and Islam must accept Toras Moshe, and only claim that it was changed or edited.
Those religions rest on the word of one man, while the Jewish emunah rests on Hashem speaking to millions at Har Sinai.
To win followers, the founders of those religions removed the difficult mitzvos, since a man cannot make a promise like the Torah's promise for shemitah.
The Sefer Torah was given to the very generation that witnessed its events, who could have exposed any falsehood, and it has come down identical letter for letter.
History witnessed by multitudes cannot be faked, which is why no one doubts George Washington while no one believes Rip Van Winkle.
The Torah is forever, and Hashem, who knows the future, cannot be said to have changed His mind.

He asks why they must accept it and answers that at Sinai something happened that never happened before or since.

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how Christianity began with one man and was reshaped by Paul, who claimed a vision, and why idol-worshipping nations accepted a message of one G-d. He then says Mohammed likewise set himself up as a new navi.

title.en: Shemitah: a promise only Hashem can make

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a new religion cannot be sold if it is hard. Shemitah would starve farmers, and only Hashem could promise a crop for three years; a man could not, so the founders of those religions removed the difficult mitzvos.

title.en: Har Sinai: Hashem spoke to millions

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the Jewish emunah, which does not rest on one man, with the revelation at Sinai, where Hashem spoke to millions and appointed Moshe as His navi before them all. He brings the passuk telling Klal Yisroel to search all of history for anything like it.

title.en: A Sefer Torah written before witnesses

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that after forty years of mann, Moshe Rabbeinu gave every Jew a Sefer Torah, so the whole generation could check it against what they had witnessed. The Sefer Torah's own laws protect it from change, and every Sefer Torah, even of long-separated communities, is identical.

title.en: Washington, Caesar and Alexander

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares George Washington, whom no one doubts, with Rip Van Winkle, a story told by one writer, and adds Julius Caesar and Alexander the Great: what multitudes experienced cannot be faked, even if small details can be. So too Toras Moshe, given to a multitude and learned day after day.

title.en: Why the nations resent the Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Torah is hard for the nations, who lack the love of the children of Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, so the Torah was made easy for them and they claimed Hashem replaced the Jewish people. He explains that the nations persecute the Jews out of jealousy, since deep down they know the Jews' greatness, as seen in Jewish advisors like Mordechai and Daniel.

title.en: The Torah is forever

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Torah promises it will never be replaced and that a navi who comes to change it is a false navi. Claiming Hashem changed His mind makes Him a liar, and with a mashal of a gift of a hundred dollars he shows that One who knows the future cannot change His mind. He closes that he will elaborate further.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the generation of the flood refused Torah and tefillah, so the waters of Torah came down as a flood, and that Cheshvan, the month of the flood, is the time to take on new learning and warm tefillah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara in Zevachim about the uproar in the world at Matan Torah and the blessing of peace. He brings a Midrash that Hashem wished to give Torah and tefillah to the generation of the flood, but they refused both. Their souls returned in later generations, and Noach, a spark of Moshe's soul, could not pray for them because they were not bound to him; Moshe later did pray and succeeded. The Mashgiach explains that Torah is water, and the waters meant for Torah became the flood. Shemini Atzeres, when one prays for rain, is a prayer for Torah, and Cheshvan, the month of the flood, opens the new learning season. He speaks of the new masechta, Yevamos, of joining Torah with tefillah, and of the Steipler's answer that Torah is true wealth. He closes on the warm weekday tefillos of the beis medrash and blessings.

en: The generation of the flood was offered Torah and tefillah and rejected both.
Noach, a spark of Moshe's soul, could not pray for his generation because they were not bound to him; Moshe later prayed and succeeded.
Torah is compared to water, and the waters meant to come down as Torah came down instead as the flood.
The prayer for rain on Shemini Atzeres is at its root a prayer for Torah, and Cheshvan, the month of the flood, is the month of Torah when the new learning season begins.
Torah must be joined with tefillah, and the generation of the flood rejected tefillah too.
Learning Torah is the greatest wealth, as the Steipler answered when asked why he was not rich.

Shemini Atzeres, when one prays for rain, is a prayer for Torah, and Cheshvan, the month of the flood, is the month of Torah that opens the new learning season. He returns to the Gemara in Zevachim: the nations feared a new flood at Matan Torah and were told it was Torah coming down.

title.en: A flood of Torah and the new masechta

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Torah is bound up with the number three and reads 'bashalom' as a flood with a shin, a flood of Torah and not of destruction. He then speaks of the new learning season and Masechta Yevamos, which demands iyun, and says that learning with hasmadah is the opposite of the flood generation's refusal.

title.en: Torah with tefillah, and true wealth

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rabbi Aharon of Karlin that Torah needs tefillah and tefillah needs Torah, and recalls that the flood generation rejected tefillah. He tells how the Steipler, asked why he was not rich, answered that he was, since Torah is the greatest wealth. He speaks of the weakness of the generation, of the compassion a Jewish heart feels for the victims of wars, as the prophet's heart went out to Moav, and of strife among the nations as a sign of Moshiach.

title.en: Yevamos, warm tefillos and blessings

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Masechta Yevamos is a tikkun bringing Moshiach, and that learning and davening help redeem Tziyon. He describes the warm weekday tefillos of the beis medrash, calls for using that gift in Cheshvan with desire for Torah and tefillah unlike the flood generation, and closes with blessings.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the generation of ikvesa dimeshicha faces the test of the akeidah, simple emunah that ignores the kushyos, and that this emunah rests on the mesorah of what an entire nation saw at Har Sinai.

abstract.en: After a short introduction by another speaker, the Mashgiach opens with emunah as the foundation of all the mitzvos: simple faith, as the grandmothers had, that Hashem alone runs the world. He shows it through Dovid HaMelech, who accepted Shimi ben Gera's curse at once as coming from Hashem. Chabakuk founded all the mitzvos on emunah, and this speaks to our generation, the heel of Klal Yisrael, which will be redeemed through emunah; the yetzer hara therefore invents new devices to tear Jews away from it. Following the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, the last test before Moshiach matches the akeidah, where Avraham, stripped of his levels, went blindly past the kushyos. The Mashgiach then brings the Yismach Moshe's answer on doubts: a mesorah of what a whole nation saw cannot be false. He closes with hashgacha pratis, inherited emunah and the light of Chanukah.

en: Emunah in Hashem is the foundation that all the mitzvos stand on, and it must be simple emunah, without philosophy.
Emunah must be strengthened every day, like food, through Shema, tefillah, sefarim and drashos; a Jew must be not only a believer but a seeker of emunah.
Our generation is the heel of the generations of Klal Yisrael, and it will be redeemed in the merit of emunah.
Since the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, the last test before Moshiach is the test of the akeidah.
At the akeidah Avraham went blindly against the kushyos, and our generation must likewise close its eyes and say Shema.
Following the Yismach Moshe, the Mashgiach explains that a mesorah of what a whole nation witnessed at Har Sinai cannot be a fabrication.

title.en: Emunah, the foundation of the mitzvos

summary.en: After a short introduction by another speaker, the Mashgiach opens with the mitzvah of emunah, which the Ramban says is greater than a mitzvah since it is the root of all of them. He describes simple emunah, as the grandmothers had, that Hashem alone runs everything and no creature has any power without Him.

title.en: Dovid HaMelech and Shimi's curse

summary.en: The Mashgiach links emunah to bitachon and asks how Dovid HaMelech became the fourth leg of the Divine chariot. He tells how Shimi ben Gera cursed Dovid as he fled Yerushalayim, and Dovid stopped Yoav, knowing at once that Hashem had told Shimi to curse; in that moment of hashgacha pratis he was raised.

title.en: Chabakuk: all mitzvos rest on emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that Chabakuk set the whole Torah on one mitzvah, emunah, and Yirmiyahu's call to search Yerushalayim for one who seeks emunah. He explains that emunah must be strengthened daily like food, through Shema twice a day, every tefillah, sefarim and drashos, and that a Jew must be a seeker of emunah.

title.en: The generations as one body; we are the heel

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Chabakuk's message speaks to our generation, ikvesa dimeshicha. He describes Klal Yisrael through the generations as one body: the dor hamidbar the head, the era of the Beis HaMikdash and tefillah lower down, and the last generation the heel, which will be redeemed through emunah, as the Midrash says on 'tashuri merosh amanah'.

title.en: New tools of the yetzer hara; the deeds of the Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the yetzer hara invents new technology and devices to tear Jews from emunah, since emunah will bring the redemption and his end. He then brings the Ramban's rule that what happened to the Avos is a sign for their children, with the examples of Avraham's descent to Mitzrayim, and concludes that the last test of Klal Yisrael before Moshiach must match Avraham's last test, the akeidah.

title.en: What was the test of the akeidah?

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what the akeidah tested, since Avraham had already let himself be thrown into the fire for his emunah against Nimrod before he ever received prophecy. He explains that a nisayon is a test that raises a person, from the word nes, a banner, so by the tenth test Avraham stood very high. He introduces 'vayar es hamakom merachok' with the picture of a Jew who wakes with fresh desire to serve Hashem, against one who wakes without any feeling.

title.en: Avraham at the akeidah: blind emunah against the kushyos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that at the akeidah Avraham's levels were taken from him and he saw Hashem from afar, in a state of small mind, open to kushyos: Hashem had promised offspring through Yitzchak and Hashem does not retract. Avraham, the first of the believers, did not look at the kushyos or the Satan's arguments; thrown down to the level of a simple Jew of ikvesa dimeshicha, he went to the akeidah with eyes closed.

title.en: Our generation's akeidah

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the akeidah to our generation, which faces the same test through kushyos about the gezeiros on Jews and books written against emunah. Hashem's double call 'Avraham, Avraham' is an expression of love for the generation that passes this test, and 'eikev' alludes to the heel. He adds that one must also believe in the chachamim and tzaddikim of the generation, and that in times of kushyos one must hold on to Avraham's emunah.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe on doubts in emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Torah was given in a way that leaves no room for kushyos. He tells of a Jew who wrote to the Yismach Moshe that he was tormented by doubts, which come from Amalek, and of the Yismach Moshe's answer: not philosophy, but the tradition handed down from a multitude who saw, which cannot be a lie, since one could not tell his child that a whole nation saw what it never saw.

title.en: What the multitudes saw cannot be denied

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Yismach Moshe, which he says is already in the Kuzari and the Rambam: one person's tale can be doubted, but no one can deny George Washington, Alexander the Great or Julius Caesar, whom millions knew. So too millions left Mitzrayim, saw the splitting of the sea and heard Hashem speak to each one at Sinai, lived forty years with the mann and the well, and received from Moshe a Sefer Torah recording it, identical among Jews everywhere.

title.en: Other faiths rest on one man; ours on a nation

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the two great religions of the world, each based on what one man said, with the Torah's own claim in Vaeschanan that no nation ever heard G-d speak from the fire. He brings the Rambam that those religions did the world a favor by building on the Torah, though in a diluted form, while Jews hold the original, because Hashem spoke face to face with each Jew, and this mesorah from Sinai cannot be falsified.

title.en: Simple emunah, hashgacha pratis and the light of Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to closing the eyes against kushyos and crying out Shema and Ani Maamin, and brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that even a straw falling from a wagon is directed from Heaven. Emunah is inherited from the Avos and lives in a Jew's heart and blood; one who ignores the kushyos is helped by Hashem. He ends with the Chashmona'im's mesiras nefesh, the hidden light of Chanukah as the light of emunah, and a wish to wait for Moshiach with clear emunah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches bochurim that Torah is the mind and tefillah the heart of a Jew's spiritual life, and that in the generation before Moshiach heartfelt, even loud, davening is what revives a person and makes his learning pure.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the two organs that give life to the body, the mind and the heart, and compares them to Torah and tefillah. From the Gemara's teaching that tefillah is the 'service of the heart' he shows that davening with the lips alone is not davening. Real tefillah needs effort and concentration, and it is the path to dveikus, which he defines as speaking with Hashem; for our generation it means pouring out one's heart. He describes the sweetness of such davening, citing Tehillim and Yedid Nefesh. Then he explains why, in the time before Moshiach, tefillah is needed even more than Torah, with the parable of a sick man who needs orange juice rather than bread and meat. A story of a young man who learned ten years 'for the cats' warns against learning to show off; learning for Hashem depends on davening well. He ends with loud davening, a Chortkov story, and a brachah to the bochurim.

en: Torah corresponds to the mind and tefillah to the heart; a Jew's spiritual life needs both, just as a body cannot live without either organ.
Tefillah is the 'service of the heart', so saying the words with the lips alone, even with their meaning in mind, is not yet davening.
Heartfelt davening brings a person to dveikus, cleaving to Hashem, which the Mashgiach describes as speaking with Him; for our generation it means pouring out one's heart to Him.
In the time before Moshiach tefillah is needed even more than Torah, and even bochurim, who must toil in Gemara, need it as part of Klal Yisroel.
Learning must be refined, for Hashem's sake and not to show off, and one cannot learn this way without davening well first.

summary.en: The Mashgiach defines dveikus as speaking with Hashem, a yichud, and says all the mitzvos are counsels to reach it. Great tzaddikim were lost in Hashem; in our low generation dveikus means pouring out one's heart, feeling that Hashem loves and listens, and this is the service of the heart.

Saying Yedid Nefesh in a rush means little, but after preparing for Shabbos properly it can be said with truth; he mentions bochurim who shed tears of love while davening.

With the parable of a sick man who needs orange juice, he shows that Klal Yisroel in its 'old age' needs tefillah, and so do bochurim who must toil in Gemara.

title.en: Ten years of learning for the cats

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Torah must be refined, learned for Hashem, not to show off with questions and answers. He tells a story from Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz about a young man who learned day and night for ten years thinking his father-in-law was listening overhead, and found only a family of cats in the attic.

title.en: Learning lishmah needs davening

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one must at least know that one learns for Hashem, and that refined learning comes only after davening well; then the Gemara is felt as holy. He brings the Beis Aharon that tefillah and learning each need the other, like mind and heart, and contrasts Moshe Rabbeinu, head of the learners, with Dovid HaMelech, head of those who daven.

title.en: Loud davening, and a closing brachah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that quiet or loud davening follows each Rebbe's root of the soul, telling of a Karliner chassid in Chortkov whose heartfelt shouting the Rebbe praised. He says that today davening is like Ne'ilah and one must daven loud to warm oneself, and ends with a brachah to bochurim going to Eretz Yisroel.

catalogTitle: The Finger of Hashem in World History; Introduc- ing The Seven Wonders

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Moshe Rabbeinu's charge to study history, and the Megillah's hidden miracle, reveal Hashem guiding all of history for Klal Yisroel, and he introduces the 'Seven Wonders of History' as proof of it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Moshe Rabbeinu's words in Haazinu, to remember the days of old and understand the years of each generation: it is not enough to remember history, one must study it. The Megillah teaches the same lesson. It contains no open miracles, only natural events, and its many details seem irrelevant until the end, when everything locks into place; this, he explains, is why it is read at night and again by day, the second time with praise and thanks. Moshe foretold the whole future of the Jewish people, and the Ramban notes that such predictions, fulfilled, prove the Torah's truth. The Mashgiach then describes the history courses of the teshuvah movement in Eretz Yisrael and lists their 'Seven Wonders of History'. He begins elaborating on the first, the eternity of the Jewish people, a prediction against all logic, and answers the claim that it was inserted later with the Septuagint.

en: Moshe Rabbeinu tells the Jewish people in Haazinu not only to remember history but to study it and understand it.
The Megillah teaches hashgachah pratis: every event in the world, big or small, is guided by Hashem toward His purpose, which centers on the Jewish people.
Moshe Rabbeinu foretold the entire future history of the Jewish people, and its fulfillment shows the truth of the Torah, as the Ramban writes at the end of Haazinu.
The teshuvah movement in Eretz Yisrael brings many people back through courses in Jewish history, among them one called the 'Seven Wonders of History'.
The seven wonders are intertwined into one wonder of wonders: convincing proof that the world is controlled by Hashem for the sake of the Jewish people.
The promise that the Jews would be an eternal nation defies all logic, unlike a forecaster's educated prediction, and still it came true.
The Septuagint, which the nations themselves possess, shows by their own account that the Torah's text was set long before Christianity, so its predictions were not inserted later.

title.en: Study history: Haazinu and the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Moshe Rabbeinu's charge in Haazinu to remember and understand the years of every generation, meaning to study history. He turns to the Megillah, read at night and repeated by day, which teaches that every event is guided by Hashem through natural means, for the sake of the Jewish people.

title.en: Why the Megillah is read twice

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the Megillah's seemingly irrelevant episodes, Vashti, the search for a queen, Bigsan and Seresh, that a yeshiva bochur would not read in a newspaper, and shows that at the end they all lock into the miracle. This, he explains, is why it is read at night and again by day: the second time one reads every detail with joy and thanks.

title.en: Moshe foretold all of Jewish history

summary.en: The Mashgiach says history must be studied with understanding, like learning a Tosafos, to discover that wars and the fortunes of nations all have a purpose centered on the Jews. In Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu Moshe foretold all that the Jews would go through, and he brings the Ramban that such fulfilled predictions prove the Torah's truth; Hashem is hidden in history and revealed through His miracles.

title.en: The teshuvah movement and its history courses

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the teshuvah movement in Eretz Yisrael, where young people searching for meaning come to organizations such as Aish HaTorah and Ohr Somayach and are convinced by courses on Jewish history. He introduces one course, the 'Seven Wonders of History', and explains that the seven are intertwined into one wonder of wonders proving that Hashem runs the world for the Jewish people.

title.en: Wonders one and two: eternity and light

summary.en: The first wonder: the Jews are an eternal nation, as promised in the Torah, surviving the great empires that oppressed them. The second: the Jews are a light to the nations, having taught an idol-worshipping world that there is one G-d; Christianity and Islam took this belief from them while dropping the difficult mitzvos.

title.en: Wonders three to seven

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the remaining wonders: the Jews' unbroken bond with Eretz Yisrael, which stays desolate without them; the teshuvah foretold before Moshiach, now unfolding after two centuries of reform; their survival as one sheep among seventy wolves; the hatred of the nations toward so small a people; and their remaining few in number, fifteen million against hundreds of millions of Yishmael's descendants, as the Torah foretold.

title.en: A prediction against logic; the Septuagint

summary.en: Returning to the first wonder, the Mashgiach contrasts the Torah's promise of eternity with a weather forecaster, who predicts only what makes sense. To the claim that such predictions were inserted later, he brings the Gemara's account of the seventy sages who translated the Torah into Greek for King Ptolemy, all making the same changes; the nations still hold this Septuagint, from centuries before their religion.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach applies the Gemara's rule that one who takes a path of temptation when another path exists is called a rasha to the use of smartphones, and teaches that the whole Torah turns on obeying the Sages of each generation.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the passuk in Yeshaya praising one who shuts his eyes from seeing evil, and the Gemara that applies it to a man who passes women washing clothes at the river. If he had another road and chose this one, Rashbam says he is a rasha even if he closes his eyes; only when there is no other way may he go. The Mashgiach applies this to a smartphone: if business truly requires it, he may use it with great care, but if a plain phone with a hechsher would do, he earns that title. He then turns to the obligation to obey the Sages of every generation: the Rambam and the passuk 'al pi haTorah', the Gemara in Eruvin, and the Gemara in Berachos on eating before Maariv. Shaarei Teshuvah explains that disobeying the Sages comes from belittling them. This, he says, is the axis of the Torah, the middle passuk of Devarim. The story of Shlomo HaMelech shows the danger of relying on oneself; one who submits to the Sages gains Hashem's help against the yetzer hara.

en: One who walks a road of temptation when he could have taken another road is called a rasha, even if he shuts his eyes and does not look.
The Mashgiach applies this to a smartphone: one who truly needs it for business may use it with care, but one who could manage with a plain phone with a hechsher falls under that title.
There is a mitzvah to obey the Sages of every generation, not only the Great Sanhedrin, including the fences and enactments they make for their time.
According to Shaarei Teshuvah, one who disobeys the Sages does so out of belittling them, and that is why Chazal treat it so severely.

title.en: Shutting the eyes, and the smartphone

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk in Yeshaya and the Gemara about a man passing women washing clothes at the river: if he had another road, Rashbam calls him a rasha even if he does not look. He applies this to a smartphone: one who truly needs it for business may use it with care, but if a plain phone with a hechsher would do, he earns that title.

title.en: The mitzvah to obey the Sages of each generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam on the passuk 'al pi haTorah', that one must obey not only the Great Sanhedrin but the Sages of every generation, including their fences and enactments. He adds the Gemara in Eruvin on 'chadashim gam yeshanim' and the Gemara in Berachos on eating before Maariv, and asks why that carries such a severe liability.

title.en: Shaarei Teshuvah: disobedience as contempt

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Shaarei Teshuvah, that one who disobeys the Sages does so because he belittles them and thinks he knows better, like the rebellious elder. He explains that one who keeps the Torah as the Sages direct is guarded by Heaven against the yetzer hara, while one who belittles them loses that help, and closes with the blessing of long days for those who follow the Sages.

abstract.en: This is a talk by another speaker (named R' Tauber in the catalog title), not by the Mashgiach. He opens with the privilege of living in a generation led by gedolim, and says the yetzer hara changed tactics: once outside persecution ended, the Jewish strength never to give in turned against the guidance of rabbanim, so that obeying them feels like a prisoner's chains instead of a soldier's duty. An army sends its strongest men to the hardest front, so this generation was trusted with the hardest test. He brings R' Mendel of Rimanov's words that the last battle before Moshiach was pushed off by 150 years, and links it to the 1960s and the rise of personal technology, which, he says, even its own makers keep from their children. He tells stories of children harmed through simple phones, and teaches five rules for one who must use a device: who, when, what, where and how.

en: The speaker says that after outside persecution ended, the Jewish power never to give in was turned against following the rabbanim, so their guidance is felt as a prison instead of an army.
He argues that an army sends its strongest soldiers to the hardest front, so this generation's hard test is a sign that Heaven trusted it.
Personal technology, he says, entered quietly like the serpent's bite, and harms people's ability to think, focus and relate to others.
One whom Hashem requires to use a device for parnassah is like a soldier assigned to the nuclear department: he must go, but he must guard himself with great care.
He gives five rules for such use: who, when, what, where and how, and stresses the 'how' that children see at home.
There is no rule that a father may and his child may not; what a parent enjoys on a device, the children will learn to enjoy.

title.en: A generation led by gedolim, facing a test

summary.en: The speaker (not the Mashgiach) speaks of the privilege of living in a generation with gedolim who lead it, says the idea of obeying them has been twisted, and describes the alarm over the new test of devices, even in Teaneck. He recalls how earlier generations struggled over Shabbos.

title.en: The yetzer hara's new tactic

summary.en: The speaker describes how easy Yiddishkeit is today, with Shabbos, kashrus and seforim all available. He says that once persecution ended, the yetzer hara turned the Jewish strength of not giving in against the young people's acceptance of their parents and rabbanim.

title.en: A soldier, not a prisoner

summary.en: The speaker contrasts a prison and an army, which look alike from outside, and says a Jew bound by the Torah should feel like a soldier, not an arrested man. He says young people answer every story with 'these are different times', and asks what kind of times they are.

title.en: The strongest are sent to the hardest front

summary.en: The speaker tells of a ba'al teshuvah who served in the Gulf War 'on the front' by washing laundry, and contrasts it with the elite soldiers sent after bin Laden. He concludes that Heaven sent this generation to the hardest front because it trusts it.

title.en: R' Mendel of Rimanov and Napoleon

summary.en: The speaker says the tzaddikim foresaw this generation, and brings what R' Shimon of Zhelichov wrote of R' Mendel of Rimanov, who wanted Napoleon to win while the Ba'al HaTanya opposed it, and who said before his passing that the last, hardest battle had been pushed off by 150 years. He links this to 1965 and the open breakdown of the street.

title.en: How technology crept in

summary.en: The speaker describes technology turning into a personal device, from the calculator to the car phone, and says the owners of the big technology companies send their children to schools without screens. He cites attention spans shrinking, and says a person emptied this way has no heart left for Shabbos.

title.en: Parnassah and the nuclear department

summary.en: The speaker takes up the claim that one has no choice for parnassah, says detailed guidelines go out of date quickly, and offers one clear approach: like soldiers who handle nuclear bombs, people carry devices that can destroy a whole home, even simple flip phones.

title.en: Stories of 'kosher' phones

summary.en: The speaker tells of a twelve-year-old boy in Monsey who was harmed by what a classmate showed him on the classmate's mother's talk-only phone, which the classmate had opened to the internet in minutes, and of a Boro Park menahel who found his own 'kosher' phone open to the internet. He says parents themselves often do not know.

title.en: When Hashem sends one into the job

summary.en: The speaker tells of a yungerman with many children who refused any job tied to the internet until his rav and a Rebbe in Monsey told him he must take one and guard himself. He compares this to a soldier ordered into the nuclear department, who goes as a hero and asks his son to say Tehillim for him.

title.en: Five rules: who, when, what, where, how

summary.en: The speaker lays out five rules for one who must use a device, says very few truly need a smartphone on their person, and stresses that even filtered email is a serious business tool, not a pleasure. He tells of a Boro Park yungerman who keeps his smartphone in the car and told his son he touches it only when he must.

title.en: What children learn, and the last battle

summary.en: The speaker says there is no rule that permits a father what is forbidden to his child, and tells of a mother whose 'harmless' smartphone her children watched her enjoy. He closes that the internet will get worse, that this is the last and hardest battle R' Mendel spoke of, and that with pride in using only what one must, this generation will greet Moshiach.

catalogTitle: The Enigma of the Survival of an Exiled Nation; Clarifying Anti-Semitism

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that the survival of a small, hated and exiled Jewish nation, its influence on the world and the endurance of its Torah were all foretold in the Torah and have no explanation other than Hashem's promise.

abstract.en: Continuing from the previous week, the Mashgiach recalls Hashem's promise that the Jews will be an eternal nation: the tochachah says He will not reject them in their enemies' lands, the Torah foretells they will remain few, and Yeshaya promises His love will never move away. He then asks why the nations hate the Jews, and answers that they know the Jews are the chosen people and superior in every field, and envy breeds hatred, as with Yosef's brothers. He reads testimony from Mark Twain, Tolstoy and John Adams on Jewish eternity and influence. Since then the Jews survived pogroms and Hitler, and Torah emerged stronger in quantity, as Moshe Rabbeinu foretold that Torah would never be forgotten. He tells of the Abarbanel, who refused to stay in Spain, and contrasts Spain's decline with Eretz Yisrael in the headlines. These wonders, like bread growing from the ground, go unnoticed only because people are used to them.

en: Hashem promised that the Jews would remain a small nation in exile yet never be destroyed, a promise only He could make.
The nations hate the Jews because they know the Jews are the chosen people and excel in every field, and envy leads to hatred.
Honest gentile writers and leaders, such as Mark Twain, Tolstoy and John Adams, testified to the eternity and unique influence of the Jews.
The Torah keeps the Jews alive; after Hitler tried to destroy it, Torah learning emerged greater in quantity, though its quality declines with each generation's distance from Sinai.
Moshe Rabbeinu foretold that the Torah would never be forgotten from the Jews, something no human being could have predicted.
These facts are among the wonders that prove the truth of the Torah and the existence of G-d; people overlook them only because they are used to them.

title.en: The promise of an eternal nation

summary.en: Continuing from last week, the Mashgiach recalls Hashem's promise that the Jews will survive every exile, bringing the tochachah in Bechukosai, the prophecy that they will remain few, and Yeshaya's promise that Hashem's love will never move away.

title.en: Why do the nations hate the Jews?

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the nations hate the Jews when other peoples' claims to superiority are ignored. He answers that they know the Jews are truly the chosen people and excel in every field, and envy breeds hatred, as with Yosef and his brothers.

title.en: Mark Twain and Tolstoy on the Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Mark Twain's description of the Jews as one percent of mankind whose influence is out of all proportion and who outlived every great empire, and then Tolstoy's words calling the Jew the emblem of eternity whom no persecution could destroy.

title.en: John Adams' testimony and the root of hatred

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how John Adams rejected a proposal to deny the Jews equal rights and wrote that the Hebrews did more to civilize mankind than any nation, teaching the world that there is a G-d. With such testimony from gentiles, he concludes, it is no wonder they envy and hate the Jews.

title.en: Surviving Hitler: Torah keeps the Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that since those writers the Jews survived Russian persecution, wars and Hitler, who targeted Torah learners first. Citing Rav Saadia Gaon that the Jews are a nation through their Torah, he shows that Torah emerged greater in quantity, though its quality declines with each generation's distance from Sinai.

title.en: A Torah never forgotten; a light to the nations

summary.en: The Mashgiach stresses that no scholar could have predicted three and a half thousand years ago that the Torah would last forever, yet Moshe Rabbeinu did, and Jews learn until old age. He adds that, as Yeshaya foretold, the nations walk by the Jews' light and kings were guided by Jewish ministers.

title.en: The Abarbanel and the expulsion from Spain

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Spanish expulsion, when thousands chose to leave with nothing rather than convert, and of Don Yitzchak Abarbanel, the king's finance minister, who refused the king's request to stay. Since the Jews left, Spain declined into insignificance, while Eretz Yisrael is on the front page every day.

title.en: Wonders we take for granted

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the blessing to Avraham that all families of the earth will be blessed through him, and calls the Jews' survival and influence one of the wonders that prove the truth of the Torah. He explains that people overlook such wonders because they are used to them, like the generation that ate the mann and was amazed that bread grows from the ground.

oneLiner.en: A talk by R' Langer, not a shiur of the Mashgiach, at a gathering on technology, urging the listeners to go against the current and adopt the rabbonim's resolutions on phones and the internet.

abstract.en: This is a talk by another speaker, R' Langer (per the catalog), given in the Mashgiach's presence at a gathering about technology before the Yamim Noraim. He asks why we pray for life and answers that life is for Hashem's sake; true life is shown by a bird that swims against the current. He tells of young men who already switched to kosher phones, brings the Avnei Nezer's reading of a father's duty to teach his son to swim, and stresses following the rabbonim, like a grafted branch that lives only while bound to the old one. He reads 'nokef etzba' as an acronym for modern devices, retells R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld's words on zealotry, tells the parable of the monkey trap and his own decision to give up his phone, and closes by reading the main takanos on phones, computers and the internet.

en: R' Langer says one asks for life because life is meant to be lived for Hashem, who has the greatest nachas from souls in a low generation.
He brings the halachic sign that a bird swimming against the current is not a treifah, and says this is what life means: standing up against the current.
Citing the Avnei Nezer, he explains a father's duty to teach his son to swim as preparing the child not to drown in the waters of this world.
He stresses that the chain of the generations holds only as long as one stays bound to the rabbonim and follows them.
He relays the rabbonim's resolutions: a kosher phone is best, a smartphone only where needed for a livelihood and kept at work, and the internet only with a filter and a rav's guidance.

title.en: Why ask for life: going against the current

summary.en: R' Langer opens in the Mashgiach's presence, asks why we pray for life before the Yamim Noraim, and answers that life is for Hashem's sake. He brings the halachic sign that a bird which swims against the current is kosher and calls that true life.

title.en: Following the rabbonim on technology

summary.en: He tells of young men who switched to kosher phones, brings the Avnei Nezer on teaching a child to swim, the grafted branch, Pinchas's zealotry, the Gemara on R' Meir and R' Akiva, and a reading of 'nokef etzba' as modern devices. He retells R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld's words on zealotry and a story of a filter expert's son.

title.en: The monkey trap and his own decision

summary.en: He tells how monkeys are caught because they will not let go of the rice in their fist, and says that for now one can still let go. He tells how he decided to give up his own phone and how a policeman let him off a ticket, and brings R' Yisrael Salanter on simply acting.

title.en: Jumping in together; the takanos

summary.en: Using the parsha of Amalek, he calls on everyone to jump in together and accept the resolutions, then reads the main takanos on kosher phones, smartphones for a livelihood, computers and the internet, and closes with a tefillah for the geulah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches Jewish women that the home, with its kedushah and the light of Shabbos, is in their hands, and that a smartphone, the fruit of the 'smart tree' of knowledge, brings tumah into it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach explains that Beis Yaakov is the Jewish home, and that Chazal call a wife 'the house'; Rav Hirsch reads the wife as a fruitful vine at the house's pillars. Sarah's tent had a cloud of Shechinah, blessing in the dough and a Shabbos lamp that burned all week. These left at her death and returned only with Rivka, because the merit of Avraham and Yitzchak was not enough: the woman is the spirit of the home and carries the light of Shabbos into the weekdays. Reb Zusha would not enter a house until the Biur was thrown out; so too a smartphone brings tumah that darkens the Shabbos lights. The tree of knowledge was a 'smart tree' bearing smartphones, and the women, whose mitzvos repair Chava's sin, are called on to clean their homes of it and build a holy Shabbos home.

en: Beis Yaakov is the Jewish home, and everything that happens in it, including the growth of the family, is entrusted to the akeres habayis, the woman of the house.
The cloud of Shechinah, the blessing in the dough and the Shabbos lamp left Sarah's tent at her death and returned only when Rivka came.
The woman is responsible for the kashrus of the home and brings in kedushah, tznius and the spirit of Shabbos, which continues into the weekdays and which a G-d-fearing visitor can feel.
A smartphone in the home brings in tumah and weekday darkness that contradict Shabbos and darken its lights.
The Mashgiach calls on the women to clean their homes of the smartphone like chametz and to build a pure Shabbos home, lighting candles with tzedakah and tefillah for their husbands and children.

title.en: The Jewish home is in the woman's hands

summary.en: After brief announcements, the Mashgiach opens with the passuk 'so shall you say to Beis Yaakov' and explains that Beis Yaakov is the Jewish home, which Chazal identify with the wife. He brings Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch on the wife as a fruitful vine at the pillars of the house, and describes Sarah's tent with its cloud, the blessing in the dough and the Shabbos lamp, all of which left at her death.

title.en: Why the blessings returned only with Rivka

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the blessings left although Avraham and Yitzchak still lived there, and answers that their merit was not enough: only with Rivka, the akeres habayis, did the Shechinah return, for she is the spirit of the house. He explains that the woman brings kedushah, tznius and the spirit of Shabbos into the weekdays, which a G-d-fearing visitor senses, and reads 'her lamp does not go out at night' as the Shabbos light that stays lit all week.

title.en: Reb Zusha, the Biur and the smartphone

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Reb Zusha stopped at the door of a house because he sensed tumah, and entered only after the host threw out Moshe Mendelssohn's Biur. He applies it to a smartphone, which brings tumah and weekday darkness into a Jewish home; on Friday night the good angel sighs at such a house and the evil angel rejoices, while a pure home raises children like olive saplings.

title.en: The 'smart tree' and the call to cleanse the home

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that women's mitzvos of challah, niddah and candle lighting repair Chava's sin of eating from the tree of knowledge, which he calls a 'smart tree' whose fruit were smartphones; a smartphone at home renews that sin and damages the bond with husband and children. He calls on the women to clean their homes of it like chametz, to light Shabbos candles with tzedakah and tefillah for husband and children, to welcome the good angel, and closes with brachos.

title.en: Second speaker: the lowest generation

summary.en: Another speaker, mostly in English, relates Rav Shimshon's question why the final generation is the lowest, and a Midrash about Yosef Meshisa, who entered the Beis HaMikdash for the Romans and then refused to go back in, dying like Rabbi Akiva. With a mashal of a father who finds his lost son, he explains that a generation far from Hashem that reaches out to Him attains a special level.

title.en: Three perspectives on digital technology

summary.en: The speaker presents three perspectives: not everyone will pass this test, as in past challenges such as Shabbos work in America and the exodus from Egypt; the technology was created by Hashem as a test specifically for Klal Yisrael; and technology is only at its beginning, so one must ask not what is wrong but what comes next.

title.en: Barzilai and inviting Hashem home

summary.en: Through Barzilai haGiladi, who was rewarded with a place at Shlomo HaMelech's table for taking in Dovid HaMelech in his time of need, the speaker says that Hashem, as it were, is desperate for people who will invite Him into their homes while the world is drawn to its devices.

title.en: Taking stock: need versus want

summary.en: The speaker urges families to take stock of their devices, filters and settings, with stories of parents who were too relaxed and of a boy who kept his filter so as not to influence others. He discusses using a device only out of need, seeing each new technology as a downgrade, and avoiding both extremes with children, and closes by recalling the mesirus nefesh of past generations.

title.en: Unity and following the chachamim

summary.en: A further speaker says the gathering itself is a kiddush Hashem and that unity forms clouds of glory. He tells of a talmid of the Avnei Nezer stranded among Cantonists on Shavuos, whose words on 'there you will be buried' his Rebbe valued: in later exile, not following the chachamim brings destruction.

title.en: Teaching children to swim; Gideon's three hundred

summary.en: The speaker brings the Gemara that a father must teach his son to swim, explained as keeping afloat against the currents of society, the Zohar that even one united congregation can bring the geulah, and the story of Gideon's three hundred who did not kneel to drink and with whom Hashem saved Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach on the pilgrims' shoes

summary.en: The speaker brings Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach's explanation of 'how beautiful are your steps in shoes': Hashem's greatest nachas comes from the hard journey up to Yerushalayim in shoes, more than from the joy inside the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Rav Meir Shapiro: his mother, Prague and Pressburg

summary.en: Stories of Rav Meir Shapiro: his mother weeping when no melamed awaited him after a move, which he called the source of the Daf Yomi idea, and his comparison of Prague, where he was shown only relics of Yiddishkeit, with Pressburg of the Chasam Sofer, who made no compromises.

title.en: The speaker's own phone; no test too great

summary.en: The speaker tells how meeting two former students whose homes were damaged by phones led him to give up his smartphone, how a police officer let him go without a ticket the morning after he decided, and a story of a Rebbe who knew a merchant's ship had not sunk because Hashem does not send a test a person cannot bear.

title.en: The chicken that was an eagle

summary.en: The speaker tells a mashal of the Vilkomir Maggid about an eagle hatched among chickens who discovered he could fly, applying it to Jews who forget they descend from the Avos and Imahos, and speaks of giving up conveniences as a korban, through which yeshuos come.

title.en: The takanos and closing wishes

summary.en: The speaker presents the takanos in the booklet: a kosher or basic phone is preferred, a smartphone only for parnassah, filtered and not used in public, and internet blocked at home. He encourages the women to strengthen one another and closes with wishes for a good year and the coming of Moshiach.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach strengthens his listeners in tefillah: davening is the service of the heart and a meeting with the King, to be done slowly, together, aloud, and without talking, especially during chazaras hashatz.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of 'make a light for the teivah': the teivah is the word, and each word of davening must be lit up with one's whole strength. His rebbe, Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, explained that the world is a flood of apikorsus and desires, and the Jew is saved by entering the teivah of tefillah. The Mashgiach recalls how loud, joyful davening by bachurim led to the founding of the Chevra Emunas Yisroel, and says davening needs constant chizuk because people treat it lightly. Tefillah is the service of the heart: it is a meeting with the King, which the Gemara calls pegiah. He tells of a simple Jew whose heartfelt Tehillim saved him from an informer. He then speaks sharply about leaving the room during chazaras hashatz and about talking in davening, and closes by asking for tefillah for the Jewish people in hard times.

en: Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, the teivah of Noach is the word of tefillah, and one must put one's whole strength into each word.
Tefillah is the service of the heart; its essence is the heart's longing and kavanah, not only the spoken words or their translation.
Davening is speaking directly to Hashem and meeting Him; the Gemara's word pegiah means an appointment with the King.
To daven well one must daven slowly, so that the heart understands each word, and together with others who want to daven.
Chazaras hashatz, instituted by the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, is a great opportunity, and walking out to chat during it is not fitting.
Talking during davening brings destruction, while not talking brings protection and blessing.
