title.en: The teivah of the word of tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of 'make a light for the teivah' as lighting up each word of davening. He cites Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz that the world is a flood of apikorsus and desires, and a Jew is saved by entering the teivah of tefillah; he adds that davening strengthens one against Amalek.

title.en: How the Chevra Emunas Yisroel began

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how bachurim davening loudly and with joy in a summer season led to a minyan in a store front in Boro Park, the start of the Chevra Emunas Yisroel. He says davening needs chizuk every few years, and brings the Gemara that people treat lightly the things that stand at the height of the world, which is tefillah.

title.en: Tefillah as the service of the heart

summary.en: From the Slonimer sefarim the Mashgiach brings that the mitzvah of tefillah is 'to serve Him with all your heart', the service of the heart, while Torah is the service of the mind. The essence of tefillah is the heart, not speech; with the Chovos HaLevavos he defines it as the soul's longing for G-d, more than knowing the meaning of the words.

title.en: Standing before the King

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Berachos that tefillah three times a day comes from a passuk in Tehillim whose word he reads as the heart pouring out. Shemoneh Esrei is in the second person, spoken straight to Hashem; he cites the Rambam and Reb Chaim on knowing one stands before the King. He tells of one who davened mincha gedolah because his heart could not wait, and brings the words of Yedid Nefesh.

title.en: Moments of hispashtus and an appointment with the King

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Shulchan Aruch that early chassidim reached hispashtus hagashmiyus in davening, and says simple people today can still merit moments of it. Pegiah means an appointment with the King of kings. He then explains how to work on it: davening slowly so the heart understands each word, and davening together with others, as Jews once used to.

title.en: The simple Jew and 'Tzam'ah nafshi'

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story told by the Beis Avraham of Slonim: a simple Jew named Ephraim, threatened by an informer for selling brandy without a permit, went to shul to say Tehillim, and at 'Tzam'ah nafshi l'Elokim' forgot his trouble and longed only for Hashem; when the police came they found nothing. He concludes that davening together with achdus lets the heart pour out.

title.en: Ramban on davening aloud; an hour and a half

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban at the end of Parshas Bo: the purpose of creation and of the mitzvos is that people acknowledge the Creator, and this is the purpose of raising the voice in tefillah and of the batei knesios. He then brings the Tanya in Iggeres HaKodesh that even working people should spend at least an hour and a half on shacharis.

title.en: Chazaras hashatz is not a break

summary.en: The Mashgiach addresses a new problem: young men walk out into the hall to chat during chazaras hashatz. He explains its greatness, instituted by the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, brings the Mishnah Berurah about following in an open siddur, and says the coffee room is part of the beis medrash; he brings the Tosfos Yom Tov that the decrees of Tach v'Tat came because of talking during davening.

title.en: The Skverer fire, the late soul, and a closing plea

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells that when the Skverer Rebbe's beis medrash burned, only the room where no one talked during davening remained, and speaks of the Tosfos Yom Tov's Mi Sheberach. He tells of a soul that came too late for a tikkun because in life it came late to davening and learning. He closes saying the tzibur davens well, and asks for tefillah for the Jewish people and the world in a time of trouble, and for Moshiach.

catalogTitle: The Exclusive Relationship Between the Jewish People and Eretz Yisroel

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that the unique history of Klal Yisroel, foretold in the Torah and full of things that contradict each other, from a land that yields only for its people to an eternal nation that is small and hated, proves that Hashem creates and runs the world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues his series on the wonders of Jewish history. Hashem told us in the Torah that Eretz Yisroel belongs only to Klal Yisroel: in golus it would lie desolate, and many nations fought over it yet none settled it, as Mark Twain described. Now that Yidden are returning it flourishes, which the Gemara in Sanhedrin calls the clearest sign of the keitz, and the Mashgiach describes how he saw this change himself. He then explains that Yidden kept the Torah through the ages; their avodah zarah came from a powerful yetzer hara, and whole communities gave their lives for emunah. Reform, which began in Germany, did not save those who left Yiddishkeit, and today a teshuvah movement is fulfilling the pesukim. Finally he shows that an eternal nation which is small, scattered and hated is a contradiction only Hashem could foretell, and that history centers around Klal Yisroel, as the Megillah shows in miniature.

en: The Torah foretold that Eretz Yisroel would be desolate while Yidden are in golus and produce for no one else; history bore this out.
The land flourishing again as Yidden return is, according to the Gemara in Sanhedrin, the clearest sign that the keitz is coming.
Yidden always kept the Torah; the avodah zarah described in Tanach came from an overpowering yetzer hara, not from abandoning the Torah.
No other people ever gave their lives in whole communities for its belief, as Yidden did throughout the ages.
The Torah foretold both that Klal Yisroel would be small, scattered and hated and that it would remain the eternal nation, two things that contradict each other in nature.
The whole of world history revolves around Klal Yisroel and its redemption, as the Megillah shows in miniature.

desolation of the land in golus
signs of the coming of Moshiach

title.en: A land that waits for its people

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Torah's promise that Eretz Yisroel belongs to Klal Yisroel alone and would be desolate in golus. He describes Mark Twain's account of the empty land and the nations that fought over it without settling it, contrasting it with today's fruitful land.

title.en: The blossoming land as a sign of the keitz

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Sanhedrin that the land producing fruit again is the clearest sign of the coming of Moshiach. He tells how disappointed he was by the empty land on his first visit and how it has grown greener every year since, and notes the country's prosperity.

title.en: Yidden kept the Torah; the yetzer hara of avodah zarah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the avodah zarah of Tanach does not mean Yidden left the Torah: it was a powerful yetzer hara, which the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah later nullified. He compares it to the yetzer hara for arayos and for money today, which can trip even an observant Jew.

title.en: Mesirus nefesh, and the Reform that began in Germany

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how whole communities chose death over giving up their belief, something no other people ever did. He then tells how the Reform movement began in Germany two hundred years ago to escape persecution, brings the Or Sameach's warning that the destruction would come from Germany, and notes that Hitler killed even those who had converted.

title.en: The teshuvah movement foretold

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes today's teshuvah movement and the fervor of ba'alei teshuvah, and shows it was foretold: the Navi's hunger to hear the word of Hashem, the Gemara in Taanis about the drizzle before the storm, and Moshe Rabbeinu's words in Devarim 30 that Yidden will return and then be gathered back.

title.en: Few, scattered and hated, yet eternal

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the pesukim that Yidden will be scattered, few in number and despised among the nations, yet will remain the eternal nation. He points out that these two predictions contradict each other and begins to frame the contradiction as X and Y.

title.en: Empires vanished; the hated nation remains

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the vanished empires of Bavel, Greece and Rome with the small, exiled Jewish people that still exists, against all logic. He explains, with Rashi's words that Eisav hates Yaakov and with Haman's argument, that the nations hate Yidden because they are different, yet could not wipe them out.

title.en: History cries out that Hashem runs the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that this unique history, with the Torah's accurate predictions, shows that Hashem creates and controls everything, alongside the instinctive emunah and the emunah received at Sinai. He brings Moshe Rabbeinu's call to study history, notes the outsized prominence of Yidden, and calls the Megillah of Purim a miniature of Jewish history.

oneLiner.en: At Kever Rachel, the Mashgiach explains that Rachel is the mother who carries the Jewish souls through exile until they are handed over to Yaakov, and that Jewish tears in exile carry great weight.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the passuk that Yaakov saw Rachel and the sheep of Lavan and rolled the stone off the well, and asks why the two are joined. Rachel, he explains, is the mother of the Jews in exile, who arouses mercy for them; Lavan's sheep were Jewish souls captive in Lavan's kelipah, and a Midrash counts Yaakov's six hundred thousand sheep as the souls he later refined in Mitzrayim. Seeing both, Yaakov wished to lighten their exile and rolled a stone off the heart of Knesses Yisrael. Since the souls were not yet ready, he worked seven years for Rachel and they stayed meanwhile with her. When Yaakov reached Eretz Yisrael her task ended, she died and was buried on the way, to resume it in later exiles. At Kever Rachel the Mashgiach asks that the time come for Rachel to bring the flock to Yaakov, tells of the river of Jewish tears seen by the Sadigura Rebbe, and closes with a tefillah for the geulah.

en: Yaakov rolled the stone because of two things together: Rachel and the sheep of Lavan.
Rachel is the mother of the Jews in exile, whose task is to revive them, comfort them and weep for them.
Lavan's sheep were Jewish souls held captive in Lavan's kelipah, which Yaakov would later refine into the six hundred thousand souls of Klal Yisrael.
Because the souls were not yet ready, Yaakov worked seven years for Rachel, and meanwhile the flock stayed with her.
Rachel died when Yaakov reached Eretz Yisrael and was buried on the way, so that she could resume her task when the Jews would go out again into exile.
Jewish tears in exile have great importance; they are the tears of Rachel.

title.en: Rachel and the sheep of Lavan

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the passuk joins Rachel and Lavan's sheep as the reason Yaakov rolled the stone. He explains that Rachel is the mother of the Jews in exile, and that Lavan's sheep were Jewish souls captive in Lavan's kelipah, which Yaakov saw and wished to ease.

title.en: Seven years with Rachel, then burial on the way

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the rolled stone as easing the heart of Knesses Yisrael, and why Yaakov worked seven years for Rachel while the souls stayed with her. Her task ended when Yaakov reached Eretz Yisrael, so she died and was buried on the way for later exiles; the shepherds' words that Rachel comes with the sheep meant the time had come to hand them to Yaakov.

title.en: At Kever Rachel: tears and tefillah

summary.en: Standing at Kever Rachel, the Mashgiach asks that the time come for Rachel to bring the flock to Yaakov and the Jews to Eretz Yisrael, stresses the worth of Jewish tears in exile with the story of the Sadigura Rebbe seeing the Ruzhiner at a river of tears, and closes with a tefillah for the geulah.

title.en: Closing

summary.en: Closing.

oneLiner.en: At Kever Rochel on the last day of Av, the Mashgiach explains Elul as the month Yaakov 'grabbed' back from Esav, traces the power of grabbing to Rochel's self-giving and to Binyamin, and calls for grabbing oneself out of today's trials through Torah together with tefillah.

abstract.en: Speaking at Kever Rochel as Av ends, the Mashgiach brings the Zohar that Yaakov 'grabbed' the month of Elul from Esav, and a Midrash about a maiden who grabbed an angel's wings and was set as Elul's mazal, Besulah. Since a mazal is the flow of influence on its month, Elul's influence is grabbing: a person should grab from the sitra achra, not be grabbed by it. He then turns to Rochel, whose soul left with Binyamin's birth, and to the Midrash where Hashem forgives Israel in the merit of her giving her signs to her sister. Binyamin, her quintessence, has the power to grab back, as on Tu B'Av when his tribe grabbed wives at Shiloh. Sitting at Rochel's grave, the Mashgiach calls for a resolution not to be grabbed by the yetzer hara, laments young men caught by electronic devices, and insists that Torah and tefillah must go together, recommending Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah before Shabbos davening.

en: Following the Zohar, the Mashgiach explains that Elul is a month Yaakov grabbed for himself from Esav's portion.
A mazal is the source of influence that flows onto its month, so the influence of Elul is the power to grab: to take from the sitra achra rather than be taken by it.
Rochel's soul left together with Binyamin's birth, so Binyamin is the quintessence of his mother.
Tu B'Av became a day of grabbing through Binyamin, whose tribe grabbed wives at Shiloh, and from then on Yaakov's portion can be grabbed back.
The Mashgiach says Torah and tefillah must go together, and that this is the only counsel for the trials of our time.

title.en: Kever Rochel and the grabbed month of Elul

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens at Kever Rochel, saying the whole area is Rochel's place, and speaks of Rochel as mother of the Jewish people. He brings the Zohar that the months were divided between Yaakov and Esav and that Yaakov went and grabbed Elul.

title.en: The mazal of Elul and the power to grab

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a Midrash that a maiden grabbed the wings of one of the fallen angels, flew up to the Kisei HaKavod and was set as the mazal Besulah, the mazal of Elul. He explains that a mazal is the flow of influence on its month, so Elul's influence is grabbing: a person must grab from the sitra achra and not let himself be grabbed by the desires of the times.

title.en: Rochel's passing, Binyamin and her plea

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rochel's soul left as Binyamin was born, and since the moment of passing holds the essence of a whole life, Binyamin is her quintessence. He brings the Midrash in which the Avos and Moshe pleaded in vain and Hashem forgave Israel for Rochel, who gave her signs to her sister, and the passuk promising that her children will return. Because Binyamin carries her self-giving, he has the merit to grab back what Esav wants for himself, since all of creation belongs to Yisrael.

title.en: Binyamin grabs: Tu B'Av and Kislev

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the war with Binyamin, the oath not to give them wives, and the advice to grab the daughters dancing at Shiloh, as in Sefer Shoftim; this was on Tu B'Av, which the Gemara counts as a yom tov for this reason. He explains that from Tu B'Av on the portion is Yaakov's, that the day became a day of grabbing through Binyamin, and that Binyamin's month Kislev also grabs days of Teves for Chanukah.

title.en: A resolution at Rochel's grave as Av ends

summary.en: On the last day of Av, sitting at the grave of Rochel, the root of grabbing, the Mashgiach calls for a resolution not to let the yetzer hara grab, which he calls the avodah of Elul that Yaakov began. He laments the fine young men who come to him caught by today's electronic devices, says breaking out takes real self-sacrifice, and that everyone is affected to some degree.

title.en: Torah together with tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that one cannot have tefillah without Torah nor Torah without tefillah, and tells of a young man who came crying to the Satmar Rav that he could not rid himself of bad thoughts. He stresses that no one can be sure when a sudden trial will come, that Torah with tefillah is the only counsel, and calls on all to enter the grabbed month of Elul grabbing with Torah and good middos, not foolishness.

title.en: Good davening and Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls good davening the best counsel and recalls great men who came to tefillah with deep seriousness, naming Rabbi Shlomo Heiman, Rabbi Yisrael Chaim Kaplan and Rabbi Reuven Grozovsky. He speaks of chevlei Moshiach, says Rebbe Elimelech nullified them through tefillah, and recommends saying Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah on Shabbos morning before davening, taking ten minutes to plead before Hashem.

oneLiner.en: At the place of Shmuel Hanavi, the Mashgiach explains why it is a place of Rosh Hashanah: here Chana's long tefillah was answered, she first called Hashem by the name Tzevaos, and Shmuel, the head of the prophets, was born.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach suggests that just as each place in Eretz Yisroel is tied to a mitzvah, the place of Shmuel Hanavi is a place of Rosh Hashanah, the day the world is conceived, since here Chana conceived Shmuel. Many laws of tefillah are learned from Chana, among them standing before the King. Eli did not know that a long tefillah is a merit, which Chana introduced; the Mashgiach adds that tefillah is something people belittle. He brings a Midrash that one can be barren in tefillah and in Torah, and says this place is a segulah for whoever finds learning and davening hard. Shmuel's first prophecy punished Chofni and Pinchas, who kept women from returning to their families. Chana was the first to use the name Tzevaos, which the Mashgiach explains as the hosts of Jewish souls. Citing the Chasam Sofer, he says Chana's tefillah was on Rosh Hashanah, and closes with a brachah for a fruitful year.

en: The Mashgiach suggests that the place of Shmuel Hanavi is a place of Rosh Hashanah, the day the world is conceived, because Chana conceived Shmuel there.
Many laws of tefillah, including standing before the King in Shemoneh Esrei, are learned from Chana.
Eli objected to Chana's long tefillah because he did not know that lengthening one's tefillah is a merit, something Chana introduced.
The Mashgiach says this place is a segulah for one who finds davening and learning hard, so that his Torah and tefillah bear fruit.
Chana was the first to call Hashem 'Tzevaos', and she used it to ask for children; the Mashgiach explains Tzevaos as the hosts of Jewish souls.
Following the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach says Chana's tefillah took place on Rosh Hashanah, which is why it is the haftarah of Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: The place of Shmuel as a place of Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions the segulah of being called up for the Rosh Hashanah haftarah, and suggests that just as places in Eretz Yisroel are tied to mitzvos, the place of Shmuel Hanavi is tied to Rosh Hashanah, the day the world is conceived, since Chana conceived Shmuel here.

title.en: Laws of tefillah learned from Chana

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that many laws of tefillah come from Chana, such as standing before the King. He describes Eli's impatience with her long davening and explains that Eli did not know that a long tefillah is a merit, adding that tefillah is among the things people belittle.

title.en: Barren in tefillah and Torah; a segulah here

summary.en: The Mashgiach cites the Chasam Sofer on the segulah of the Rosh Hashanah maftir and a Midrash that one can be barren in tefillah and in Torah. He says the place of Shmuel Hanavi is a segulah for whoever struggles to daven and learn, and recalls that Chana's tefillah brought Shmuel, the head of the prophets.

title.en: Chofni and Pinchas, and the name Tzevaos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shmuel's first prophecy was a punishment of Chofni and Pinchas, who delayed the women's offerings and kept them from their families. He then notes that the name Tzevaos first appears in Chana's tefillah, ties it to netzach and hod, and explains it as the hosts of Jewish souls, so that this is a place to be helped with children and with fruit in Torah and tefillah.

title.en: Chana's tefillah was on Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows from the word 'vehaya' and from the Chasam Sofer on 'miyamim yamimah' that Chana davened on Rosh Hashanah, when Elkanah and Chana came to Shiloh. Those at this place take on the aspect of Rosh Hashanah, of Chana and of Shmuel, and he closes with a brachah for a bright, fruitful year.

title.en: Niggun

summary.en: A niggun is sung, followed by a brief remark recalling that the niggun was sung in camp in the days of Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz.

catalogTitle: הקדמה - תכלית דרך הבעש"ט' תכלית ספר תניא. פרק א' - “משביעים אותו תהי צדיק וכו'”

oneLiner.en: Opening a new Tanya series, the Mashgiach sets out the aim of the Baal Shem Tov's path and of the Tanya, then begins chapter one with the oath given to the soul, 'be a tzaddik and do not be a rasha', and the contradictions it raises.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that what matters is what Chassidus taught, not its history. The Baal Shem Tov brought love of Hashem to the simple Jew, while his disciples, above all the Baal HaTanya, carried deep teachings; the Baal HaTanya also wrote the Shulchan Aruch HaRav. The Tanya, unlike other Chassidic seforim arranged on the parsha, is an orderly course in serving Hashem, meant to show why keeping the Torah is 'very close' and simple, as its title page says. Beginning chapter one, he explains the braisa that the soul is made to swear to be a tzaddik and not a rasha: a shevuah comes from sheva, seven, binding all seven forces of creation, and is related to shefa, a flow of strength from above that stays with the soul. He then raises the Tanya's question from the Mishnah 'do not be a rasha in your own eyes' and brings the Gemara's five categories and the Raya Mehemna on the tzaddik and the beinoni, leaving the resolution for the next session.

en: The Baal Shem Tov taught that every Jew is dear to Hashem and can cleave to Him through davening, chesed and ahavas Yisrael, even without being a talmid chacham.
The Tanya is not a collection of Torah thoughts on the parsha but an orderly course of chapters on how to be an eved Hashem, whose first chapters lay the foundations.
The aim of the Tanya, as its title page signals, is to show why keeping the Torah is simple and 'very close', though most people find it hard.
The word shevuah comes from sheva, seven: an oath binds a person with all seven forces with which Hashem created the world, leaving no way out.
The oath given to the soul before birth is not meant to be remembered; it is a flow of strength, shefa from above, that accompanies the soul and helps it fulfil its mission.

The braisa's demand to consider oneself a rasha seems to contradict the Mishnah 'do not be a rasha in your own eyes', and logic pulls both ways: sadness blocks joyful service, while self-satisfaction leads to lightheadedness.

title.en: Teachings over history; the Baal Shem Tov's path

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the history of Chassidus is not the point, illustrating with a quip about a maskil who wanted to show off historical trivia. He then describes the Baal Shem Tov's accomplishment: bringing love of Hashem to simple Jews, who can cleave to Hashem through davening, chesed and ahavas Yisrael.

title.en: The Baal HaTanya among the Maggid's disciples

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the deep teachings carried by the disciples of the Baal Shem Tov and the Maggid of Mezritch, with the Baal HaTanya foremost in understanding. He tells how the Maggid assigned him to write a Shulchan Aruch, most of which was burnt, and how its every word sheds light on the Gemara's sugyos.

title.en: The purpose and structure of the Tanya

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Tanya, called Likkutei Amarim, has one aim stated on its title page: to show why keeping the Torah is 'very close' and simple. Unlike the other Chassidic seforim of its generation, built on Torah said on the parsha, it is an orderly course of 53 chapters, whose first fifteen or twenty lay the foundations of avodas Hashem.

title.en: The oath to the soul; shevuah and sheva

summary.en: After giving tzedakah to begin the new learning, the Mashgiach reads the braisa that opens chapter one: the soul is made to swear to be a tzaddik and not a rasha. Citing the Ramban, he explains that shevuah comes from sheva, the seven forces of creation, so an oath binds a person with all of creation and all his seven middos.

title.en: An oath that gives strength; lashon hakodesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what an oath the soul forgets can accomplish, and answers that its impression stays and gives strength, as Avraham's oath gave Eliezer strength on his mission. He then explains that lashon hakodesh, unlike arbitrary languages, reveals the meaning of things in their words, as shulchan comes from 'sent'.

title.en: Shevuah and shefa: strength from above

summary.en: Since beis and pei, letters of the lips, interchange, the Mashgiach links shevuah with shefa, showing the class a white beis inside a written pei. The oath is a flow of strength from above that accompanies the soul on its individual mission; he explains hashpa'ah through a slanted roof that lets rain flow down, as for a mikveh.

title.en: Seven in avodas Hashem; an oath with no escape

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that spiritual empowerment comes in sevens: the seven blessings of Krias Shema, the Sheva Brachos, the seven blessings of the Shabbos Shemoneh Esrei. Since 'naaseh adam' made man contain all of creation, an oath leaves no opening to escape, which is why even one suspected about money is not suspected about an oath.

title.en: The contradiction: rasha in one's own eyes?

summary.en: The Mashgiach presents the Tanya's question: the Mishnah says not to be a rasha in one's own eyes, and logic too pulls both ways, since sadness prevents serving Hashem with joy while feeling good leads to lightheadedness. He begins the answer with the Gemara in Berachos listing five kinds of people, from the complete tzaddik to the beinoni.

title.en: Raya Mehemna: the ra subordinate; three judges

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Raya Mehemna on Mishpatim: a 'tzaddik v'ra lo' has some bad in him, but it is subordinate to the good. He describes the inner tribunal of yetzer tov and yetzer hara, where the tzaddik hears only the good judge, the rasha only the bad, and the beinoni both, and brings Rabbah who called himself a beinoni, leaving the reconciliation of these Gemaras for the next session.

oneLiner.en: Speaking to bachurim about to learn in Eretz Yisroel, the Mashgiach explains that being in the land is not enough: one must be 'planted' in it, feel its holiness every day as on Rosh Hashanah, and keep one's dirah a holy place.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a story of a sick tzaddik who asked a traveler to Eretz Yisroel to sip water for him, since one who prepares to go is already 'Eretz Yisroel'. Addressing bachurim going to learn there, he warns that one can be in the land without being in it, as people walk the streets on Shabbos with no tie to Shabbos; Eretz Yisroel is the Shabbos of the world, and one must be planted in it like a tree, not lie there like a log. Every mitzvah and every sin there is multiplied. From the Ruzhiner and the passuk 'from the beginning of the year' he shows that Eretz Yisroel is a constant Rosh Hashanah. He brings the Chasam Sofer, the great tzaddikim who were not allowed to go, the Torah beginning and ending with the land, the Hafla'ah and Chasam Sofer on Moshe's tefillah, and the diamond parable of 'a good and wide land'. He closes by asking the bachurim to keep their dirah holy, with rules for sleep and order.

en: One can go to Eretz Yisroel and still not be in Eretz Yisroel; being there requires zechus and a real connection to the land.
Eretz Yisroel is the Shabbos of the world, and a mitzvah or a sin done there weighs far more than elsewhere.
A Jew in Eretz Yisroel must be planted there like a tree, with love of the land and awareness of its responsibility, not lie there like a cut log.
Eretz Yisroel is Rosh Hashanah: in it a person is judged every day, so every day there must be lived with the seriousness of Rosh Hashanah.
One must not grow accustomed to Eretz Yisroel; it should feel new each day, as Torah should.
The bachurim's dirah in Eretz Yisroel should be holy, with rules for curfew and enough sleep so they can daven and learn with a fresh mind.

Moshe's tefillah to enter the land
tzaddikim who could not reach Eretz Yisroel

title.en: Going to Eretz Yisroel, but being there?

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a sick tzaddik who drank water from the mouth of a traveler to Eretz Yisroel, then addresses bachurim going there to learn. Citing the meraglim, he warns that one can go to the land without being in it, and calls Eretz Yisroel the Shabbos of geography.

title.en: Planted, not a log

summary.en: From 'plant them on the mountain of Your inheritance' the Mashgiach gives the parable of a log that does not blossom in spring because it was never planted. He compares Eretz Yisroel to Shabbos, where every mitzvah, and every sin, counts many times over.

title.en: Eretz Yisroel is Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Ruzhiner asked a man leaving for Eretz Yisroel whether he could live every day as Rosh Hashanah, and explains that in Eretz Yisroel one is judged daily because the land was created first. He brings the Chasam Sofer that the land makes a tzaddik greater and a rasha worse, laments idle bachurim there, and quotes the Chasam Sofer on giving one's soul to rise to the land.

title.en: A zechus earlier generations lacked

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Torah of Eretz Yisroel is a different kind of Torah, contrasts today's overnight flight with the mesirus nefesh of earlier travelers, and notes that the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Vilna Gaon and the Chofetz Chaim were held back from going while this generation is allowed. He then brings Rashi that the Torah opens with Bereishis to show the land belongs to the Jews.

title.en: Immersing before entering the land

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the last words Moshe wrote in the Torah speak of the land, so the Torah begins and ends with Eretz Yisroel. He brings a tzaddik's teaching that water surrounds the land on four sides so one immerses before entering, and warns that the Satan invests there, as seen in the machlokes and pashkevilim on Yerushalayim's walls.

title.en: Kiddush, and Moshe's tefillah in the land

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the light of Eretz Yisroel to the holiness of Shabbos and of a tzaddik's kiddush, recalling the Satmar Rebbe's kiddush. He then brings the Hafla'ah that Moshe prayed to be able to pray, and the Chasam Sofer's answer why Moshe did not say this during his forty days in heaven: the ground of Eretz Yisroel is holier than the heaven above chutz la'aretz.

title.en: A diamond the size of a walnut

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how the small land can be called 'wide' and answers with the parable of a costly plot in Manhattan versus a diamond the size of a walnut. He describes feeling every step there, and from Rashi on 'and He gives it to you' teaches that one must not grow accustomed to the land, just as Torah must feel new each day.

title.en: The dirah that was a kiddush Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a bachur who goes with good intentions and stays away from parties and machlokes can feel the different light in learning, davening and Shabbos. He recalls that the bachurim's dirah in Yerushalayim was known as a refined place, a kiddush Hashem, and notes he heard it has recently declined, with late nights and idle talk.

title.en: Takanos for a holy dirah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks the bachurim to renew the old standard: rules for a curfew, quiet and seven or eight hours of sleep, so they can daven properly and learn with a fresh mind. A Jew's home should feel like Shabbos, with the Shechinah in it, and he closes with a brachah for the holiness of Eretz Yisroel.

oneLiner.en: Opening his study of Shir Hashirim, the Mashgiach explains why this song of love between Hashem and Klal Yisrael belongs to Shlomo HaMelech alone, and who Shlomo was: the king whose days and whose Beis HaMikdash were a foretaste of the time of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by asking why Shir Hashirim is called 'asher liShlomo', belonging to Shlomo, and answers that no one else could carry the song of love between Hashem and Klal Yisrael in both directions. It is a song of love, which is why it is said on Shabbos and why the Sfas Emes ties it to Pesach; it has no plain meaning and must be read only as a mashal. Song comes from feeling loved, and Shlomo, called Yedidyah, was so united with Hashem that his name became the name of the King of peace. The song is kodesh kodashim like the place of the keruvim, and Shlomo said it the day he finished the Beis HaMikdash, a day like Shemini Atzeres and the days of Moshiach. Its destruction on Tisha B'Av was tied to Shlomo, who returned as Yirmiyahu and will again become Shlomo. The Mashgiach ends with Shlomo's unmatched wisdom and his role as Hashem's poet.

en: Shir Hashirim is 'asher liShlomo': it belongs to Shlomo, since only he could convey the song of love from Hashem to Klal Yisrael and back.
Shir Hashirim is a song of love, which is why it fits Shabbos and Pesach, the days of love.
Shir Hashirim has no plain meaning; one rises at once above the mashal of chosson and kallah to the nimshal.
Shir Hashirim is kodesh kodashim because, like the Holy of Holies with its keruvim, it is the place of the chosson and kallah.
Shlomo said Shir Hashirim on the day he completed the Beis HaMikdash, the dwelling of the chosson and kallah, and his era was a foretaste of the days of Moshiach.
Tisha B'Av is the opposite of Shemini Atzeres, and the soul of Shlomo who built the Beis HaMikdash returned as Yirmiyahu who saw its destruction.

candidateTopics: love between Hashem and Klal Yisrael

title.en: Why the song is 'asher liShlomo'

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that unlike 'shir hamaalos leDavid', Shir Hashirim says 'asher liShlomo', and explains that the song belongs to Shlomo, since no one else could carry the love song between Hashem and Klal Yisrael in both directions. Therefore, before learning it, one should come to know who Shlomo was.

title.en: A song of love for Shabbos and Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shir Hashirim is a song of love and therefore said on Shabbos, a day of love without a korban chatas, and on Pesach, the Yom Tov of Avraham and chesed, as the Sfas Emes says. It has no plain meaning, only remez, drush and sod, and singing it requires the contentment of knowing one is loved.

title.en: Love that brings song; Shlomo the beloved

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that song flows from love: the angels, Klal Yisrael at the Yam Suf, and the Chareidim's Yedid Nefesh. Shlomo, beloved of Hashem and named Yedidyah, was so united with Hashem in love that 'Shlomo' in Shir Hashirim means both Shlomo HaMelech and the King to whom peace belongs.

title.en: Kodesh kodashim and the Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rabbi Akiva's words that Shir Hashirim is kodesh kodashim and explains them through the Holy of Holies, where the two keruvim are chosson and kallah. Shlomo said Shir Hashirim on the day he finished the Beis HaMikdash, which is called a kallah, the home of the chosson and kallah.

title.en: Shemini Atzeres, the point in the middle

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shemini Atzeres is the climax of the year: all the Yomim Tovim circle around it, and it is the complete yichud of Hashem and Klal Yisrael, alone without the nations, a sample of the days of Moshiach. Its ushpiz is Shlomo HaMelech.

title.en: Shlomo's era, a foretaste of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem has not yet had full nachas from His world, as the Midrash on 'yismach Hashem bemaasav' says, and no person has ever reached all he wished, except Shlomo, of whom it says he achieved everything he desired. He then tells that on the morning after the Beis HaMikdash was completed Shlomo slept late, and the destruction was decreed.

title.en: Tisha B'Av, Yirmiyahu and Shlomo

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tisha B'Av is the opposite of Shemini Atzeres, and that Shlomo, who built the Beis HaMikdash and wrote Shir Hashirim, returned as Yirmiyahu, who saw its destruction and wrote Eichah. Masechta Taanis ends with Chamishah Asar B'Av and the passuk 'tze'enah ur'enah... bamelech Shlomo', since in the future Yirmiyahu will again become Shlomo and sing Shir Hashirim.

title.en: Shlomo's greatness in Tanach

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that 'Shlomo HaMelech', eight letters, is tied to Shemini Atzeres, and its spelled-out letters equal Tisha B'Av in gematria. He then reads the pesukim in Melachim about Shlomo's kingdom, his peace and his rule from Tifsach to Azah, and contrasts the conquerors who took the world by war with Shlomo, who won it with wisdom.

title.en: Shlomo's wisdom and his song

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Shlomo's peace without the sword, his wisdom beyond all others as the Midrash explains the names in the passuk, and the fifteen generations from Avraham to Shlomo like the full moon. He concludes that of Shlomo's three seforim Shir Hashirim is the highest, since Hashem appointed him as His poet to carry the songs between the chosson and the kallah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why Shir Hashirim is the 'holy of holies' and the crowning tenth song: it shows that even the bond of chassan and kallah in this world can be raised to holiness, and it was written by Shlomo HaMelech to console Klal Yisrael in galus with the promise of their closeness to Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rashi's introduction: Shlomo HaMelech foresaw the exiles and wrote Shir Hashirim as the song of a 'living widow' longing for her Beloved. He recalls that every 'Shlomo' in the sefer also means Hashem, and explains Rabbi Akiva's statement that Shir Hashirim is holy of holies with a pshat of Reb Feivel on the olah and the shelamim: a Jew, whose body is of kelipas nogah, can sanctify worldly things, and Shir Hashirim reveals this by using the love of chassan and kallah as its mashal. He then shows that among the ten songs, and in every set of ten in the Torah, the tenth is tied to chassan and kallah. Shlomo, the fifteenth generation and the full moon, knew the decline would follow and wrote the sefer as a consolation for the galus. The Mashgiach explains why Shir Hashirim has no pshat, why it belongs to Shlomo, and reads 'Yishakeini' as dveikus of spirit with spirit, which Klal Yisrael prefers to the 'wine' of the seventy nations.

en: Shlomo HaMelech foresaw the long galus and wrote Shir Hashirim so that Klal Yisrael, like a 'living widow' whose husband is far away, would remember their first closeness and know Hashem has not abandoned them.

A gentile can bring only an olah, which goes entirely to Heaven, while a Jew can bring a shelamim that is eaten, because a Jew can sanctify worldly acts; Shir Hashirim, by using the love of chassan and kallah as its mashal, shows that this world too can be elevated.
Of the ten songs, Shir Hashirim is ninth in time but tenth in importance, and in every set of ten in the Torah the tenth is connected with chassan and kallah.
Shlomo was the fifteenth generation from Avraham, the full moon of Klal Yisrael; knowing the decline would begin after him, he wrote Shir Hashirim as a consolation for the darkness of galus.
Unlike every other passuk, Shir Hashirim has no pshat; the Mashgiach says it may not be learned according to its literal meaning, and the early commentators explained it entirely by sod.
'Yishakeini' expresses dveikus of spirit with spirit, the bond Klal Yisrael has with Hashem and holds dearer than all the 'wine' of the seventy nations.

title.en: Rashi's introduction: the living widow

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Rashi's introduction: Shlomo foresaw exile after exile and wrote Shir Hashirim in the voice of a 'living widow' longing for her Beloved, so Klal Yisrael would know Hashem has not abandoned them. He recalls from the previous week that the sefer is a dialogue between Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, and that 'Shlomo' means both the king and the King of peace.

title.en: Holy of holies: olah, shelamim and this world

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rabbi Akiva's words that Shir Hashirim is holy of holies, and explains them with Reb Feivel's pshat on the Midrash of north and south: a gentile can only bring an olah, a Jew can bring a shelamim, because a Jew's body is of kelipas nogah and can be sanctified. Shir Hashirim uses the love of chassan and kallah as its mashal and so shows that this world can be elevated, and he adds Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's mashal of the king who asked the baker for one pure loaf.

title.en: The tenth song and chassan and kallah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Targum's list of ten songs, in which Shir Hashirim is ninth, and explains that by importance it is the tenth, as order in time and order in importance can differ. He shows that the tenth of the ten maamaros, of the ten dibros and of Avraham's ten trials (the Akeidah, which brought about Yitzchak's zivug) is each tied to chassan and kallah, and so is Shir Hashirim.

title.en: The king's songs and the full moon

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a mashal of a king who sent away his queen: they exchanged songs, and their wise child joined them into one song, Shir Hashirim, which opens with the queen's praise of the king. He then explains that Knesses Yisrael is the moon receiving light from the sun, which waxes until the fifteenth of the month, and therefore the main Yomim Tovim fall on the fifteenth, while Shavuos is the continuation of Pesach.

title.en: Shlomo, the fifteenth generation

summary.en: Following the Midrash, Shlomo is the fifteenth generation from Avraham, the fullness of the moon, and the decline down to Tzidkiyahu and the churban begins after him. Knowing this, he wrote Shir Hashirim as a consolation for Jews in galus, just as he prepared a hidden chamber under the Beis HaMikdash where Yoshiyahu later hid the aron.

title.en: Pshat, drash and why Shir Hashirim has no pshat

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes commentators, especially the Ibn Ezra, who sought pshat even against Chazal, and relates a saying comparing Rashi, the Ibn Ezra and the Ramban. He explains that while every passuk has a pshat, Shir Hashirim has none and may not be learned literally; the early commentators, including the Ramban's commentary, explained it entirely by sod.

title.en: Yishakeini: the kiss as dveikus

summary.en: The Mashgiach begins the first passuk, where Knesses Yisrael sings to Hashem, and brings Rashi that she says it in galus and widowhood, longing for the closeness of before. He explains that a kiss is dveikus of spirit with spirit, as shown by Orpah, whose kiss was not genuine, and Ruth, who clung to Naomi because both had Jewish souls.

title.en: Why Shir Hashirim belongs to Shlomo

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how Shir Hashirim is Shlomo's when the Midrashim say it was sung at the sea and at Matan Torah, and compares Tehillim, which contains psalms said before Dovid. He answers that each Jew's neshamah has its own portion in Torah, as in the Midrash where Moshe heard Hashem say a halachah of the parah adumah in the name of Rabbi Eliezer; so Shir Hashirim belongs to Shlomo's neshamah even when said earlier.

title.en: Better than the wine of seventy nations

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'ki tovim dodecha miyayin': yayin equals seventy, and Hashem's love is dearer to Klal Yisrael than everything the seventy nations offer when they urge the Jews to join them and escape the persecutions of galus. He ends with the death by a kiss, as with Moshe, when the soul leaves the body in the pleasure of dveikus with Hashem.

catalogTitle: ביאור מהות צדיק רשע ובינוני. ארבע קליפות הטמאות. גוף ישראל מקליפות נוגה.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, through the opening questions of Tanya chapter one, that tzaddik, beinoni and rasha are defined by whether the yetzer hara still lives in a person, and then begins the teaching of the two souls of every Jew and the four klipos, the body of a Jew coming from klipas nogah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's questions: how Iyov could say Hashem created tzaddikim and reshaim when the angel never announces it before birth; how anyone can be a beinoni if a sinner is a rasha at the moment he sins; and how Rabbah could call himself a beinoni. He shows that counting mitzvos and aveiros is only a label for judgment on Rosh Hashanah, like the 'tzaddik' and 'rasha' of a din Torah. The true definition is the three judges: a tzaddik has killed his yetzer hara, as David HaMelech said his heart was empty; a rasha hears only the yetzer hara; a beinoni hears both. He then speaks of the rare tzaddikim placed in each generation, of gilgulim, and tells the Yismach Moshe's memories. Finally he begins the two souls, explaining klipah through the four shells of a walnut, the fourth, nogah, being the body of a Jew that can become holy.

en: Calling a person tzaddik, beinoni or rasha by his majority of mitzvos or aveiros is only a convenient label for how he is judged on Rosh Hashanah, not what he is in essence.

Every person has two judges in his heart, the yetzer tov and the yetzer hara, and Hashem decides; a tzaddik has rendered his yetzer hara powerless, a rasha hears only the yetzer hara, and a beinoni hears both and must choose.
Rabbah knew he had never sinned, yet considered himself a beinoni because the yetzer hara was still there and he had to guard against it.
True tzaddikim are few; Hashem placed them in every generation as its leaders, and some are sent down again not to repair anything but for the sake of their generation.
Every Jew has two souls, one from the side of klipah and sitra achra, clothed in the blood, which is the animal life he shares with every creature.
Of the four klipos, the fourth, klipas nogah, is like the edible skin of a walnut kernel; the body of a Jew comes from it and can be turned to holiness.

title.en: The Tanya's questions on tzaddik and beinoni

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's questions: how Iyov could say Hashem created tzaddikim and reshaim when the angel does not announce it before birth, and how anyone can be a beinoni if a sinner is a rasha while sinning. He asks how Rabbah, whom the Angel of Death could not approach while he learned, could call himself a beinoni, and adds that even one who fails to rebuke others or neglects learning Torah is called a rasha.

title.en: Counting mitzvos is only a label for judgment

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that the childhood measure of mitzvos against aveiros cannot define these levels. He brings the Gemara in Rosh Hashanah about the three books and explains that the terms there are only for judgment, like the 'tzaddik' and 'rasha' of a din Torah, who are named only for that one case.

title.en: Three judges: the true definitions

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the yetzer tov judges tzaddikim, the yetzer hara judges reshaim, and both judge beinonim, and builds the picture of three judges with Hashem deciding. A tzaddik like David HaMelech has killed his yetzer hara, a rasha like Pharaoh has lost his yetzer tov, and a beinoni hears both; this is why Rabbah thought himself a beinoni. He explains 'my heart is a chalal within me' as an empty chamber of the heart.

title.en: Few tzaddikim, beinonim and gilgulim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that real tzaddikim are few, placed in every generation, the 'tzaddik yesod olam' with thirty-six beneath him, and they have no choice; most people are beinonim even if they count as tzaddikim on Rosh Hashanah. He speaks of souls returning in new gilgulim, brings the Lechovitcher's reading of 'one who sleeps in the cemetery', and explains that great tzaddikim come down for their generation and remember earlier lives, while others forget so that their choice remains.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe remembers his gilgulim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells, as written by the Yitav Lev, that his grandfather the Yismach Moshe remembered being a sheep of Yaakov Avinu, showed a mark from his staff and remembered his niggun, and remembered being in the desert at the dispute of Korach, where he was neutral. He explains that Korach was a great tzaddik who made a small mistake, and that tzaddikim remember because they have no choice to lose.

title.en: Sent down without choice; a question on gilgulim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells that the Apter Rav remembered serving in the Beis HaMikdash, and says some are sent down as tzaddikim without choice and some as reshaim without choice, while the general population can go either way; the few tzaddikim are leaders for those who want to be honest Jews. He sums up that the Tanya's questions show the levels are not yet understood, and answers a listener's question about gilgulim and those without a share in the World to Come by recommending Takanas HaShavim.

title.en: Two souls and the four shells of the walnut

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads that, following Rav Chaim Vital, every Jew has two souls, learned from the plural 'neshamos', the first from the side of klipah. He explains klipah through the walnut of 'el ginas egoz', with its four shells, and says the world, created through the four letters of Hashem's Name, has shells to break through, like the four barriers Yechezkel passed in his vision and the keruvim guarding the Tree of Life.

title.en: Kedushah and the other side

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the world has two sides, kedushah and tumah, and one cannot stand in both. He brings Rashi that kedoshim means separated, and 'al tigshu el isha' with Targum Onkelos's 'side', and the Kotzker's lesson that one indulging in desires cannot expect to understand Torah; therefore what is not holy is called the sitra achra, the other side.

title.en: Klipas nogah, the blood and the animal soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the fourth klipah, nogah, is like the edible skin of the kernel and like the priah of the milah, a shell that can become holy, and the body of a Jew is from it. The first soul is clothed in the blood, which carries life as in every animal, with the four bad traits; he sums up that a Jew has a yetzer hara, his biological being, and a yetzer tov that lets him resist his desires, which no animal can do.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains 'Yishakeini mineshikos pihu' as the bond with Hashem through learning Torah, which is also the Jewish people's true weapon, and reads 'L'reiach shemanecha' as the fragrance of Hashem's miracles above nature that even the nations must sense.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach returns to 'Yishakeini mineshikos pihu': the Torah is G-dliness itself, so one who learns is truly bound to Hashem, and he ought to feel its great sweetness, as the Ohr HaChaim writes and as Dovid HaMelech says. The kiss is the Shechinah speaking through a Jew's mouth in Torah and tefillah. With the Midrash he explains that the Oral Torah, renewed below and sent upward, is dearer than the Written Torah; that 'neshikah' means hashakah, a joining like two mikva'os; and that it means 'neshek', weapons. The Torah is the Jews' weapon: the miraculous survival of Jews in Eretz Yisrael comes only through those who learn, and Shlomo HaMelech's sixty warriors were sixty masechtos. Rashi reads the song as Klal Yisrael in exile remembering Sinai. On 'L'reiach shemanecha' he explains shemen as eight, above nature, connects it to Chanukah and Shavuos, and shows how Hashem's miracles spread like poured oil, so the nations hate Israel out of jealousy and some come to convert.

en: Because the Torah is G-dliness itself, a Jew who learns is truly joined to Hashem, and the Torah should be tasted as the greatest sweetness.
The 'kisses of His mouth' are the Oral Torah, which the Midrash calls dearer than the Written Torah because it is renewed on earth and goes up to Heaven.
'Neshikah' also means hashakah, contact like that of two mikva'os, so through Torah a Jew becomes one with Hashem.
'Neshikah' also means 'neshek', weapons: the Torah is the Jewish people's ammunition, and their survival in Eretz Yisrael is only in its merit.
Shemen is related to shemoneh, eight, the level above nature, which is why miracles, Chanukah and the giving of the Torah are bound to eight.
Hashem's miracles for Israel spread like the fragrance of poured oil, so the nations must acknowledge them, and they hate the Jews out of jealousy.

title.en: Torah as a kiss: bond and sweetness

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Torah is G-dliness itself, so learning bonds a Jew to Hashem, and he should feel its great sweetness, as the Ohr HaChaim and Dovid HaMelech say. The kiss is the Shechinah speaking through a Jew's mouth in Torah and tefillah.

title.en: Oral Torah, and hashakah like a mikveh

summary.en: From the Midrash the Mashgiach explains that the 'kisses' are the Oral Torah, dearer than the Written Torah because it is renewed below and rises to Heaven, and that neshikah means hashakah, as water joined to a mikveh becomes part of it. Through Torah a Jew becomes one with Hashem, though in our generation few feel that sweetness.

title.en: Torah as the Jews' weapon in Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Midrash reads neshikah as 'neshek', weapons. The Mashgiach describes the hidden miracle of Jews living among hostile Arabs, recalls that the nations did nothing in the Holocaust and how Rommel was stopped, and concludes that the true army defending Israel is those who learn Torah.

title.en: Shlomo's sixty warriors and Rashi's reading

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how Shlomo HaMelech's sixty sword-bearing warriors fit with his having had no sword, and answers with the Midrash that they are sixty masechtos: Torah is the Jews' weapon. He then brings Rashi, who reads the song as Klal Yisrael in exile recalling Hashem's closeness at Sinai and awaiting its return with Moshiach.

title.en: 'L'reiach shemanecha': fragrance of poured oil

summary.en: On the third pasuk, the Mashgiach explains 'shemen turak' as precious oil whose fragrance is sensed only when it is poured from vessel to vessel, and brings Rashi: Hashem's name spread through the miracles in Egypt, and the 'alamos' are the nations, some of whom loved Him and converted.

title.en: Seven and eight: nature and above nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts yayin, seventy, the nations rooted in the seven days of creation, with shemen, from shemoneh, the eighth level above nature on which Hashem leads Israel. He shows this in the counting toward Shavuos, the Chanukah miracle of oil burning eight days, the eighth pasuk of Tehillim 19 about Torah, and the third month in both halves of the year.

title.en: Miracles today and why the nations hate Israel

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Torah is eternal, so the miracles of Krias Yam Suf are seen today too, and their fragrance forces the nations to acknowledge them. He explains that the nations hate even assimilated Jews because they know Israel is the chosen people, citing the Meshech Chochmah on Germany, and that some gentiles have the courage to convert.

oneLiner.en: On the pasuk 'your oils have a good fragrance', the Mashgiach explains that Hashem's miracles and all holiness are hidden like silent oil, yet the final redemption will come with open wonders, and the memory of past miracles keeps Jewish love of Hashem alive even in times of concealment.

abstract.en: Continuing Shir Hashirim 1:3, the Mashgiach teaches that miracles and holiness are hidden: the Mishkan's beams were covered, and Elisha's staff failed because Gechazi publicized the miracle. Only rarely, as in a story of the Sanzer Rav in Oberland, does a tzaddik reveal a wonder to sanctify Hashem's name. From the Midrash on oil, which pours silently and does not mix, he turns to the Jewish people, who may not mix with the nations; the return under Nechemiah came without miracles because of foreign wives. He weighs the Rambam's Moshiach, who needs no miracles, against the Raavad's, and argues the Rambam's is greater, since moving every Jewish heart is the greatest wonder. With the Yismach Moshe he shows that a promise made with Hashem's Name cannot be lost, explains why Chanukah lights stand below ten tefachim, and closes that remembered miracles keep emunah alive in hester panim.

en: Hashem's miracles, like all holiness and good deeds, are normally hidden, and an open miracle is the exception, used only to sanctify Hashem's name.
The Jewish people, like oil, do not mix with others, and the return for the Second Beis Hamikdash lacked miracles because many had married foreign wives.
The Rambam's Moshiach, who is known by his deeds rather than by miracles, is the greater Moshiach, since the greatest miracle is to bring Hashem into a Jewish heart.
A promise Hashem makes with the Shem Havayah stands above time and cannot be cancelled by sin, so the final redemption will come with miracles and wonders.
Jews keep loving Hashem even in times of hester panim because they remember the miracles of Yetzias Mitzrayim, Chanukah and Purim.

title.en: Miracles are hidden, like a fragrance

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the third pasuk of Shir Hashirim, 'your oils have a good fragrance', and explains that Hashem's miracles, like all holiness, are hidden and only their fragrance comes out. He brings the gold-covered beams of the Mishkan, which Rashi explains as tznius, and Elisha's staff, which failed because Gechazi talked about the miracle on the way.

title.en: The Sanzer Rav in Oberland

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Sanzer Rav came to a wedding in Oberland, a non-Chassidic region of Hungary, and revealed the hidden origin of the chasan, a wonder he showed because there they did not know there is a Ribono shel Olam. He then restates the rule: such openness is the exception, the open miracles of Yetzias Mitzrayim were so the world would know Hashem, and holiness is always in tznius.

title.en: Oil that is silent and does not mix

summary.en: From the Midrash the Mashgiach explains that poured oil makes no sound, and that oil does not mix: a drop of water in a full glass of oil pushes out a drop of oil, as a word of foolishness pushes out a drop of Torah. He applies this to the Jewish people, who may not mix with the nations, and shows that the return for the Second Beis Hamikdash came without miracles because of foreign wives, whom the people sent away at Nechemiah's word, contrasting this with today's assimilation.

title.en: The Rambam's Moshiach and the Raavad's

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam that Moshiach need not show miracles and is recognized by his deeds, and the Raavad who disputes this and expects great wonders. He argues that the Rambam's Moshiach is the greater one, since the greatest miracle is to bring Hashem into a Jewish heart, and that so great a Moshiach is needed for a people sunk in the fiftieth gate of impurity.

title.en: Gathering the exiles with one word

summary.en: Illustrating the Rambam's sign of gathering the exiles, the Mashgiach pictures Moshiach calling out on 47th Street and everyone leaving their shops open to follow him. He compares this to Moshe Rabbeinu's sign 'pakod pakadti', whose power was that the words entered Jewish hearts, and brings the tradition that at Moshiach's shofar even the worst meshumad will run after him.

title.en: Where the Beis Hamikdash will stand

summary.en: The Mashgiach points out that the place of the mizbe'ach must be exact, yet today nobody knows it, and every group would bring its own view; Moshiach will say one word and all will accept it. Recalling Nechemiah again, he concludes that although the Rambam makes miracles no requirement, the plain meaning of the pesukim and Midrashim is that there will be great miracles.

title.en: A promise made with Hashem's Name

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks whether our generation, worse than that of the Second Beis Hamikdash, will merit miracles. He brings the Gemara that Israel deserved miracles in Ezra's days but sin caused, the pasuk 'ad ya'avor amcha Hashem', and the Yismach Moshe's answer that a promise made with the Shem Havayah is above time and cannot be cancelled, and the final redemption is promised that way.

title.en: Chanukah lights below ten tefachim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that although the Shechinah never descends below ten tefachim, the Chanukah light is lit below ten, in the public domain, at night, on the left side and in the darkest season, all places where the forces of impurity rule. The seforim say it kindles the light of Moshiach, who will come down to the lowest Jews and lift them up.

title.en: Loving Hashem in times of concealment

summary.en: Returning to the pasuk, the Mashgiach says the Chanukah miracle came through oil, which does not mix, to purify Klal Yisrael, and reads 'alamos' as from 'he'elem', concealment: Jews love Hashem even in hester panim, as after the destruction in Europe. Their emunah holds because they remember the miracles of Yetzias Mitzrayim, Chanukah and Purim, whose fragrance still remains.

oneLiner.en: On the pesukim 'al ken alamos ahevucha' and 'moshcheini acharecha', the Mashgiach explains how Klal Yisroel loves Hashem with self-sacrifice and youthful zeal, and how even in galus Hashem brings them into His inner chambers and they rejoice with Him.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach learns Shir Hashirim 1:3-4. He first reads 'alamos' as 'al mos', unto death: throughout galus Jews gave their lives for Hashem, from the war against the Hellenists at Chanukah to the battle against the Communists in Russia and, in his day, against Reform and Conservative, at a time with no single leader for Klal Yisroel. A second reading is youthfulness: serving Hashem with zerizus, unlike the lazy man of Mishlei; he urges bochurim to use their years of youth, to keep growing in yiras shamayim, and to check the motive behind every kulah. A third reading has 'alamos' as the nations: souls from Sinai born among goyim smell the 'fragrance' of the miracles and convert. On 'moshcheini acharecha' and 'hevi'ani hamelech chadarav', he explains, with Rashi and the Midrash, that even in galus Hashem reveals new depths of Torah, as with Rabbi Akiva and Yechezkel, that His glory is in every shul, and he closes with the Midrash of the couple who took each other along.

en: 'Al ken alamos ahevucha' is read as 'al mos': throughout galus Jews loved Hashem to the point of giving their lives for Him.
In today's galus the main war is fought by Jews against Jews who abandoned the Torah, and the absence of a single leader of Klal Yisroel is one of the signs of ikvesa d'meshicha.
'Alamos' also means youthfulness: serving Hashem with energy and zerizus, and the years of youth are worth far more than later years.
Every kulah needs checking: one must ask whether it comes from the truth or from a leaning of the yetzer hara, and only a real danger, not a remote fear, excuses one from serving Hashem.
Some gentiles have Jewish souls from Sinai; they feel a drive toward Hashem, sense His miracles like a spreading fragrance, and come to convert, while the other nations remain indifferent.
Even in galus Hashem brings Klal Yisroel into His chambers: new depths of Torah were revealed in galus, through Rabbi Akiva, Yechezkel's vision in Bavel and the Talmud Bavli.
Hashem's glory is in every shul; one who does not see it must believe it, and treat the shul, a mikdash me'at, with awe.

title.en: 'Alamos': loving Hashem unto death

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'al ken alamos ahevucha' together with 'ki alecha horagnu kol hayom' and explains that Jews gave their lives for Hashem throughout galus. His example is Chanukah, when Hellenized Jews tried to force Greek culture on Klal Yisroel and Matisyahu's few fought the many.

title.en: Today's war: Jews against Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that from Russia onward the main war against Torah Jews has come from Jews: the Communists, and now Reform and Conservative in Eretz Yisroel. He laments that there is no single leader of Klal Yisroel as in his youth, calls this a sign of ikvesa d'meshicha, and says one must cling to Yiddishkeit and to the true gedolim.

title.en: 'Alamos': youthful zeal in avodas Hashem

summary.en: A second reading from the Midrash: Jews love Hashem with youthfulness, full of energy and zerizus. The Mashgiach brings the tefillah in Berachos, the opening of Shulchan Aruch and Shlomo HaMelech's field of the lazy man, then tells bochurim that the years of youth are the key to their lives and that one must keep growing in yiras shamayim or slip back.

title.en: Checking every kulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mesilas Yesharim that every kulah needs checking and explains that one must ask whether a leniency comes from the truth or from a leaning toward the yetzer hara. With the lazy man who says there is a lion on the road, he distinguishes a real danger from a remote fear, which must not keep one from davening.

title.en: 'Alamos': the nations and the gerim

summary.en: A third reading: 'alamos' are the nations. The Mashgiach explains that some gentiles carry Jewish souls that stood at Sinai; they find no rest until they come back to their root, and the fragrance of Hashem's miracles draws them, like Rachav, Rus and Yisro. The other nations stay passive and say Hashem no longer cares for the Jews, but Jews in galus hold on to Him with emunah and bitachon.

title.en: 'Moshcheini acharecha' and remembering the old love

summary.en: The Mashgiach learns Shir Hashirim 1:4 with Rashi: Klal Yisroel asks Hashem to draw it after Him, recalls how He brought them into His chambers, and even in galus, as a 'living widow', rejoices in remembering His love, like a kallah who remembers her chassan's gifts. He brings the love of following Hashem in the desert and the Clouds of Glory, the reason for Sukkos.

title.en: Hashem's inner chambers in galus

summary.en: With the Midrash that Klal Yisroel's faults come from its neighbors, the Mashgiach explains that in galus Hashem brought Jews into His inner chambers: Rabbi Akiva was shown what was not revealed to Moshe, Yechezkel in Bavel saw the Merkavah and that the Shechinah had come with the Jews, and the Talmud Bavli and the secrets of Torah were revealed in galus out of Hashem's compassion.

title.en: Emunah: Hashem's glory in every shul

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that one who does not feel the sweetness of Torah and avodah must have emunah. He brings the Midrash 'who came into the beis haknesses and did not see My glory', and the seforim that 'nifteichu hashamayim va'ereh mar'os Elokim' spells emunah: one who does not see must believe. He speaks of awe in shul, a mikdash me'at, and of thanking Hashem for being let in.

title.en: The couple who took each other along

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Midrash of a childless couple about to divorce; the husband let his wife take the most precious thing in the house, she took him, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai blessed them with children. He adds a teshuvah of the Chiddushei HaRim on such a case and a report he heard that the Sanzer Rav gave such a brachah, and applies 'nagila v'nismecha bach': in galus Klal Yisroel takes Hashem along.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the self-serving kindness of the nations, whose animal soul comes from the impure klipos, with a Jew's ability to act purely for Hashem, and then opens Tanya chapter two: the Jew's second soul is 'truly a part of G-d above'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews that a Jew's animal soul comes from klipas nogah, which can be elevated, while that of the nations comes from the three impure klipos; therefore, as the Gemara says, the kindness of the nations is a sin, done for themselves. He shows the opposite with Yaakov's seven years for Rachel, which seemed like a few days because his love was spiritual, like a tzaddik's longing for a mitzvah. Love for a thing one consumes is really self-love, and even tzedakah or martyrdom can be for oneself; a Jew can lift his compassion and even his eating to be for Hashem. Answering a question, he digresses to the Zohar: Rachel is the aspect of Yovel, of return and redemption, explaining theft, the Hebrew servant, Shabbos, Chanukah, Yaakov's grief at Rachel's death and Migdal Eder. Finally he opens Tanya chapter two: the Jewish soul is G-dliness 'mamash', breathed from Hashem's inwardness.

en: A Jew's animal soul is from klipas nogah and can be elevated; that of the nations is from the three impure klipos and cannot, so their kindness is done for themselves.
Yaakov's seven years seemed like a few days because his love for Rachel was spiritual, like a tzaddik's longing to do a mitzvah.
Most human love is self-love; even giving tzedakah or giving one's life can be for one's own satisfaction or fame.
A Jew's compassion also comes from the animal soul, but he can work on himself to act purely for Hashem, and even his eating can be elevated.
Following the Zohar, Rachel is the aspect of Yovel, return to the root and redemption, which is why Yaakov worked seven years for her.
The Tanya's word 'mamash' is exact: the second soul of a Jew is actual G-dliness, breathed from Hashem's inwardness.

title.en: Klipas nogah and the kindness of the nations

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews that a Jew's animal soul is from klipas nogah, which can be raised to good, while that of the nations is from the three impure klipos, as in the Eitz Chaim. He brings the Gemara in Bava Basra that the kindness of the nations is a sin, since they cannot act purely for Hashem.

title.en: Yaakov's seven years for Rachel

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why seven years of waiting seemed to Yaakov like a few days, and explains that his love for Rachel was spiritual, like Rav Nachum of Chernobyl longing for the esrog or a person building a sukkah. Yaakov's kiss was like kissing tefillin.

title.en: Loving oneself versus loving Hashem

summary.en: With the man who 'loves chicken', the Mashgiach shows that most love is self-love. He contrasts tzedakah given out of love of Hashem with giving to calm one's own feelings or to win honor, explains 'chesed le'umim chatas' this way, and says a Jew can lift his compassion to be purely for Hashem.

title.en: Exceptions, and elevating a steak

summary.en: Answering a question, the Mashgiach says exceptional individuals among the nations carry sparks of Jewish souls, as with converts. He explains that a Jew's eating, from klipas nogah, can be elevated when done for Hashem or used for learning, while forbidden food cannot be raised until the days of Moshiach.

title.en: Rachel and Yovel: everything returns to its root

summary.en: Bringing the Zohar on Yaakov's seven years, the Mashgiach explains Yovel as return to the root: every person's portion holds sparks only he can elevate. A thief takes another's portion, and a Hebrew servant, who lost the forty days of Torah, falls to a shifchah; Shabbos returns him, and Yovel frees even one who wishes to stay.

title.en: Chanukah as Yovel; Rachel and Moshiach

summary.en: Going off on a tangent before Chanukah, the Mashgiach explains with the Me'or Einayim that wicks and oils not lit on Shabbos are lit on Chanukah: souls Shabbos cannot lift, Chanukah, the eighth like Yovel, can. Rachel, who unites Klal Yisrael, is the shofar of Moshiach and the ingathering, buried near Beis Lechem, and Yaakov worked seven years to reach Yovel through her.

title.en: Rachel's death and Migdal Eder

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Yaakov himself offered the seven years, and brings the Zohar that Rachel's death was his greatest suffering: he felt the geulah taken away. He then brings the Targum Yonasan and the passuk in Michah that Migdal Eder is where Moshiach will be revealed, Hashem's consolation to Yaakov, and takes a question about Leah.

title.en: The second soul: G-dliness 'mamash'

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter two and stresses that every word is exact, so 'mamash' means actually. Unlike the animal soul shared with all creatures, the second soul is G-dliness itself; he brings the Zohar that Hashem, the Torah and Yisrael are one, the passuk 'vayipach b'apav', the bracha Elokai neshamah, and that one who blows, blows from within himself.

title.en: Neshamah and breath; 'alu b'machshavah'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that neshamah also means breath, a person's inwardness, as seen in Rus's kiss of Naomi against Orpah's. He then reads that Yisrael 'arose in thought' first, the reason for creation, and notes the Tanya writes 'by way of a parable' here, since Hashem's thought is unlike ours.

oneLiner.en: On the words 'we will rejoice in You', the Mashgiach explains that a Jew's joy on Yom Tov is in Hashem Himself, that the Jewish people live through the Yomim Tovim, and that the Chanukah lights bring the Shechinah and the light of Moshiach down to the lowest souls.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues with Shir Hashirim, 'we will rejoice in You, we will recall Your love more than wine'. A person with strong emunah sees Hashem's hand in every salvation, and an upright Jew rejoices more in the closeness to Hashem than in the salvation itself. Through the Midrash, Shlomo's 'in You' explains Dovid's 'in it' in Hallel: the joy is in Hashem, not the day. Each Yom Tov carries its own light, best felt by learning its halachos, which warm a Jew more than wine. Citing the Rambam on the calendar, he shows that Klal Yisrael exists through the moadim. Purim and Chanukah are weekday festivals that give a boost in galus. Chanukah lights, lit below ten tefachim, on the left, in the public domain, in the darkest season, bring the Shechinah to fallen souls, as the story of the Chozeh of Lublin and an informer shows.

en: An upright Jew rejoices less in the salvation itself than in the closeness to Hashem that he felt through it.
The joy of Yom Tov is in Hashem, not in the day; the nations' holidays are empty eating and drinking.
Learning the halachos of each Yom Tov before it lets a Jew feel its light, and they warm him more than wine.
The Jewish people exist through the moadim; without them they would have died out spiritually.
On Chanukah the Shechinah comes down below ten tefachim to the most extinguished souls, and the light of Moshiach is revealed in the lights.
